I think anecdotes are best discarded in favor of data. And I tried to do this once a while ago, although this article could use an updating with more recent statistics: https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2012/06/07/safety-is-an-expensive-illusion/

The summary is that biking is SO GOOD for you, and not really all that dangerous in the big picture, that it has an effectively negative level of danger. i.e. your lifespan and healthspan increase when you do it.

But, if you’re in a rough urban area you gotta treat it like a hockey game where YOU are the puck and every moving thing is trying to hit you. So have the literal flashing lights installed on your bike in all directions, and have your figurative radar running on high as well, especially at every curb cut and intersection.

With proper awareness, you should be able to make it almost impossible for a car to hit you even if they are trying to do so (which of course they aren’t), because you’re riding so defensively.

It sounds harsh, but this is also the same thing it takes to be a good CAR driver and avoid accidents over a lifetime of driving.

I just tallied up our non-house net worth yesterday and we’re at $1.1M. Hopefully I can early retire very soon (age 48 with a rather high paying job, but one that varies throughout any particular day from “great” to “rage quit”).

But also what strikes me is the persistent assumption that everyone needs to own a house. I’ve never owned a house and never even lived in one as an adult. I do own a boat however, which is like a tiny house, that we’ve lived on for 7 years. Renting a small apartment is perfectly valid.

I would suggest to your commenter that he explore the “tiny house/dwelling” movement. Changing the size of your home is often an even easier way to save than location arbitrage. Humans don’t need really need as much space as they think (many average suburban homes feel “mansion-sized” to me).

I recently bought my first home using the little known hack called “marry an electrician and then get a house with all knob and tube wiring, because no one else will want it due to the wires being old, even though if they were going to burn the house down they likely would have by now.”

Yup. Homes that need remodeling and new plumbing or electrical can be had for hundreds of thousands less in hotter markets. Having the trade or skills to do the work will save so much money.

I’ve added probably between $20k and $75k in value to each of my homes in these ways–always spending way less than the value returned by either doing most of the work myself or contracting out after many bids and significant time considering the design. I’ve never had a house sit on the market. All have gone under contract at about ask or over in a few days or less.

What I’ve appreciated about the Moustachian philosophy (at least from what I can tell) is that it doesn’t assume that we humans deserve to get everything we want and right now!

I’m actually a compulsive debtor in recovery, and reading blogs like this one and books like “Your Money or Your Life,” are very helpful tools for me. My past ridiculous and childish thoughts about money included:

~I deserve this ~Everyone else is doing it, I should be able to as well ~It’s my right ~I shouldn’t have to work and save. I shouldn’t have to sacrifice or make difficult choices.

These thoughts and the silly and financially damaging actions they lead to are not just the affliction of those who are compulsive, but are the foundational philosophy for our consumerist culture.

Just because I live in the U.S., doesn’t mean I deserve to be able to buy a house; especially when I did NOTHING during my pre-recovery days to save for one.

The amazing news is, however, that even though I got into recovery and began to practice sound financial principles only 10 years ago, my hubs and I own a great home in a dream location. We went from overspending each month by about $1,500 (today we’d be almost $250,000 in debt – and that doesn’t include interest payments!) to being worth over $1.5 million (this does include the estimated value of our home).

I work in my dream career and make 2/3 as much money as my hubby, but work 1/4 the time he does (this is the way we both like it).

All this to say that once you turn the ship around, once you begin to change even the smallest behaviors with money to align with Moustachian ideas, it doesn’t take long at all to see HUGE results.

Thanks, Mr. Moustache and all who embrace FIRE and principles of financial sanity! Natalie :^)

I had been ‘living’ in San Francisco as a flight attendant in a 3 bedroom with 18 roommates for $375/mo. I had begun making an excel of places I thought I would like to live and move to then the pandemic hit and it forced me to move as I was laid off. I made a list of requirements including drivable in 2 hours to a major airport/hub or closer if I commuted (I don’t have to go to work every day). It needed to be affordable housing, community-based, good internet (my parents live in Alabama and it’s not available where they live), things for me to do (entertainment), and in a climate with 4 seasons (Alabama has hot or wet, SFO has damp and less damp). I used best places which has a quiz that also asked some other good questions and I decided I probably wanted some kind of university town so there was 24 hour services (because sometimes I work nights) as that would be good for me. I then converted my Honda crv to a van and road tripped and stayed a few days to a week in each area I was considering. When I got to my current town of Harrisonburg Va I fell in love with it. As others have said, the first half of this article (the FRED graph of average sales prices across the US) is statistically questionable and has the feel of “see? housing is actually affordable, you’re just wrong to be looking at actual sales prices in your area”. As you mention, it’s a national average, when all RE markets are local, so it’s unclear what it means at all. Another distortion is that the FRED data comes from FHA, which means that it excludes cash sales and sales with jumbo loans. This distortion tends to result in lower home prices than you see when looking at, say, the Case-Schiller data. Even if you average over the whole country.

But I’m glad I ground through that part because the rest of this has some really practical advice for how to find somewhere to live. There is a classic old Raptitude post “Most Lives are Lived by Default” which suggests that probably your current location is a side-effect of your job, or school, or relationship, and that you could do better if you actively tried to find the “right” location for you. Unfortunately the article provides no advice for _how_ to do this; it mostly suggests moving to a different neighborhood in your current town, with the assumption that you have a good idea of whether you want to be closer/further to nightlife or grocery stores or bike paths or whatever, and you just need to pull the trigger.

But for somebody who is near-FIRE, or “FIRE except for housing”, it’s hard to figure out where to even start. These resources are a great way to filter for locations that are financially reasonable and also in the right part of the country. Another thing I did was keep an eye on r/financialindependence and r/fatfire to see if anybody posted cool understated places to live. Chattanouga popped up, as did Kansas City MO, and Asheville NC.

In 2020 I visited a pile of such cities, as well as big ones like Philly and Portland and NYC, by going on AirBNB and finding a spare room that I could rent for a month or more. In the Portland area I wound up doing this for several months in a row, since it’s a huge place and you can change locations dramatically without leaving the metro area.

When I first started doing this I would always look to stay in whole houses, but this is the wrong approach! Aside from not distorting housing markets by using SFHs as hotels, you actually want to find a place with a host who you can talk to about the city and who can tell you about different neighborhoods. And if you rent spare rooms for long periods, it’s a surprisingly affordable thing to do. Especially as you can often meet people who are willing to let you stay with them without going through a fee-skimming platform like AirBNB.

This strategy might only be practical for single light-travelling digital nomad types but I encourage anybody to seriously consider it.

Thanks for the Albuquerque shoutout! It’s not a perfect place to live, but if you like being outside, it’s hard to do better for what it costs to live here.

FIRE is often about making different choices than everyone else to emphasize the things that really matter to you. You rent a small apartment close to work instead of buying a McMansion in the exurbs. You bike or walk instead of driving a 3-row SUV. You cook at home instead of eating out. You go to the library instead of the movie theater…

…and you move to New Mexico instead of Colorado.

If you’re still working, the national labs are solidly above-average employers that emphasize work-life balance. The outdoor recreation is almost as good as Colorado, and Durango is only a few hours away if you want bigger mountains. There’s a nice airport, a zoo, great museums, and 3 Costcos. The weather is great: cooler than Phoenix in the summer, warmer than Denver in the winter, and sunny almost all the time. Plus, the state is doing lots to support working families, with subsidized daycare and free college tuition.

So if you’re discouraged about how much it costs to live in Bend or Boulder, make less popular choice and check out New Mexico.

As a former Coloradoan, newly adopted New Mexican I can reiterate Joel’s statements. NM isn’t perfect but I feel like I have greater access to outdoor recreation here in NM than I did in the Front Range of Colorado, plus much less people to compete with. There are slightly more sunny days, so I can’t complain about that either.

I’m in Santa Fe, which is pretty comparable to many parts of Colorado regarding cost of living and the weather feels nearly identical to Colorado with our almost 7000′ elevation. Santa Fe punches above it’s weight as a city in regards to culture, restaurants, and museums. There is a good bit of tourism that feeds into that, but the restaurant scene is pretty great. The history of the region keeps me engaged as I continue to learn more about the area.

I keep eyeballing the affordability of Albuquerque and the offerings of a city that is 5x the size of Santa Fe, but Santa Fe fits the bill for now

The key thing, as this article exemplifies, is to EXAMINE both reality, and your own assumptions. So much “can’t afford a house” mania is based on vague unexamined feelings, and vague media-based proclamations. When you cut through that with a bunch of facts and self-examination . . . the world opens up. As this piece shows. In our case, a limiting factor (we thought) was the “must be close to family” idea. Then we realized that 1. family members keep making plans and moving without consulting us, so why base our whole lives on their (temporary) locations? 2. once we did the math and realized how often we “see family” it became clear that 3 visits a year with a couple of family events each time would cover all the hanging-out time we do, anyway. YMMV.

We love to see these people! But in reality, they’re all busy, they move around, and there’s a limit to everyone’s time. So now we are free to live mostly in Europe, where we prefer to be (and where it’s cheap to live a great, low-footprint life), and not feel disloyal because of some presumed idea of “being too far away from family.” We see them as much as ever did! Now it’s just during our annual out-and-back migration. So yeah: really, truly examine everything that seems to be liming your choices.

I think the one thing you missed calling out is how this is especially relevant to FIRE folks who are no longer working. Many of these lower cost cities don’t have the high paying jobs that really helps us along the way.

Personally I went the route of moving to a small apartment and renting in a HCOL city to maximize my income in my younger years. Now that I’m coming up on 40, I’ve moved to a small town in MN and enjoying the much lower cost of living.

The other cool aspect of this idea is that you can live in a very neat neighborhood within these type of towns. For example, I’m living in the heart of the historic neighborhood within walking distance of two lakes and downtown for super cheap. If I had done that in any moderate cost of living city, I’d pay 5-10x as much for housing. So while it’s a small town, it’s still very walkable & bikeable because I’m not stuck out in some suburban wasteland.

Building a company with a cofounder puts you through pressures nobody warns you about, plus the usual startup whiplash. Noah was our co-founder at Alertive Healthcare, our previous startup. He led product, engineering and design teams. He thinks like an engineer. The question he asks reframes the entire problem, and then he proceeds to build the answer.

Here’s the problem he found. Every physician in an ambulatory clinic runs against a clock, and the tell is the glancing. The wall clock. The watch. The timer in the screen’s corner. Patients catch every one of those looks, and they read them. Noah fixed it with an app, and he fixed it elegantly.

Article’s below. See whether his solution works for you. Full disclosure: Noah is a friend. I was paid no cash, no coins, no crypto and no farm eggs to write this. I just think he’s onto something.

I originally built Haptica Timer for my wife, who is a physician.

Like many clinicians, she spends much of her day moving from one patient visit to the next. She is constantly balancing two responsibilities that can sometimes feel at odds: being fully present with the patient in front of her while also staying aware of a demanding clinic schedule.

She did not want to keep looking at the wall clock. She did not want to glance at her phone or repeatedly raise her wrist during a conversation. Even when those actions are completely innocent, they can make a patient feel rushed or leave them wondering whether the physician is still listening.

What she needed was simple: a quiet way to understand how much time had passed without visibly checking the time.

That was the starting point for Haptica Timer.

The original idea was to create subtle vibration cues that could be felt on the wrist without interrupting a conversation. Just as importantly, the timer needed to repeat automatically.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

A clinician should not have to remember to start another timer before every appointment or continually manage an app throughout the day.

Instead, the timing pattern could follow the natural rhythm of the clinic schedule, repeating from one visit to the next.

The goal was never to force every patient encounter into a rigid block of time. Some appointments need more time, and physicians must always be free to respond to what the patient needs.

The goal was simply to give clinicians a private sense of where they were in the visit, reduce the need to manually track time, and help the day move more smoothly without taking attention away from the patient.

The rest of this article is written by Jorge Sanchez, one of my former co-founders at Alertive Healthcare.

A patient is explaining something important.

The appointment may have started as a routine follow-up, but another concern has surfaced. It deserves attention. At the same time, the clinician knows the visit is beginning to run long and that another patient is waiting.

This is a normal part of medicine. Patient visits do not always follow a predictable path.

The challenge goes beyond simply keeping appointments short. It is remaining engaged with the person in front of you while still respecting the time of every patient who comes afterward.

Most clinicians develop their own ways of managing this. They glance at the clock, check the computer, look down at a watch, or try to estimate how much time has passed.

None of these approaches is necessarily wrong, but they’re all rather visible.

Patients may notice when attention shifts, particularly during emotional, personal, or complicated conversations. Even a quick glance can change the feeling in the room.

At the same time, losing awareness of time can affect the rest of the clinic day. A few additional minutes across several appointments can create longer waits, less time for documentation, hurried transitions, and increasing pressure on both clinicians and staff.

The problem is not the clock itself. The problem is needing to continually look for it.

A traditional timer is designed to capture your attention.

It makes a sound, displays a notification, lights up a screen, or requires you to look at it. Those features are useful in many settings, but they are not always appropriate during a medical visit.

An audible alarm would interrupt the conversation. A phone notification could feel out of place. A visible countdown could become another thing competing for the clinician’s attention.

The better solution was a less noticeable timer.

A subtle vibration could provide awareness without changing the conversation. The clinician could feel that a certain amount of time had passed and decide what, if anything, to do with that information.

That cue might prompt the clinician to summarize the discussion, confirm the care plan, address the patient’s final concern, or decide that the conversation needs to continue.

One of the most practical parts of Haptica is its ability to run repeating timers.

Clinic schedules often follow a regular cadence. Appointments may be scheduled in 15, 20, 30, or 40-minute blocks, sometimes with a short period between visits for documentation or transition.

Once the timing pattern is configured, the timer can repeat automatically.

This means the clinician does not need to start a new timer before every patient. There is no need to repeatedly open the app or remember to reset it as the day progresses.

For example, a physician might choose to receive one gentle cue when most of the visit has passed and another near the scheduled end. The timer can then pause briefly and begin the next cycle automatically for the following appointment.

This repeating pattern is important because it allows the timer to support the workflow without becoming another workflow to manage.

The experience is less like operating a stopwatch and more like maintaining a quiet awareness of the clinic’s rhythm.

A typical appointment may include reviewing concerns, gathering relevant history, performing an examination, discussing options, answering questions, agreeing on a plan, documenting the encounter, and preparing for the next patient.

When time awareness is lost early in the visit, the final portions can become compressed. The clinician may have less time to explain the plan, complete documentation, or transition thoughtfully to the next appointment.

A discreet timing cue can help the clinician recognize where they are in that process.

It may provide an opportunity to move from information gathering into decision-making, begin summarizing the plan, or identify a concern that deserves a separate follow-up rather than trying to address everything at once.

The repeating timer also reduces the small amount of mental and operational effort involved in managing separate timers throughout the day. Once configured, it can continue through the clinic schedule with minimal interaction.

During a routine follow-up, a subtle vibration lets the physician know that most of the scheduled time has passed.

Nothing interrupts the conversation. The patient does not hear or see anything.

The physician may begin bringing the visit together by reviewing the plan, confirming the next steps, and asking whether there is one final concern that needs to be addressed.

The cue does not end the visit. It helps the physician recognize that it may be time to transition naturally toward a conclusion.

During another visit, the vibration occurs while a patient is discussing something emotional or unexpected.

The physician feels the cue but chooses not to act on it.

The conversation continues because the patient needs more time.

This is an important part of how Haptica is intended to work. It provides awareness, and leaves the clinician to decide what the moment requires.

On a busy day, small delays can build quickly.

A few extra minutes across several morning appointments may become a significant delay by the afternoon. Patients wait longer, staff members work to catch up, documentation may accumulate, and the clinician may begin to feel increasingly rushed.

A repeating timer does not solve every scheduling or workflow challenge.

It can, however, provide a consistent sense of time throughout the day without requiring the clinician to repeatedly manage it.

That awareness may help identify when a visit is drifting, when it is time to begin summarizing, or when a concern may be better addressed through a separate follow-up.

Even when the physician decides to continue the visit, that decision is made with a clearer understanding of where the day stands.

Being present does not require completely losing awareness of time. In some cases, greater time awareness may make it easier to remain present.

When clinicians know where they are in a visit, they may feel less pressure to mentally track the clock. They can focus more fully on the patient and make a deliberate decision about whether to continue, transition, or arrange additional time.

The timer stays in the background. Clinical judgment remains at the center.

We did not want to create another complicated productivity system.

Clinicians already work with numerous systems, alerts, documentation requirements, and administrative tasks. Haptica was designed to address one specific problem without adding another layer of complexity.

It does not need to dominate the visit or become another screen to manage. The less attention it requires, the better it supports the reason it was created.

The purpose is to give clinicians one small, private signal that helps them use their time and judgment more intentionally.

#8688. Nearly 150 Doctors Walked Off the Job at a Hospital With $6 Billion In Revenue

According to the 2026 Medscape Physician Compensation Report, average physician pay reached $386,000 this year, up 3% from 2025 and enough to outpace the 2.7% core inflation rate.

Eight specialties crossed half a million dollars, led by orthopedic surgery at $611,000. 53% of physicians said they feel fairly compensated individually, the highest share in years. All wonderful news.

However, 61% of physicians still believe the profession as a whole is underpaid, and the average workweek barely budged. 63% of physicians blame bureaucratic work and electronic health records for their burnout. 14% of physicians say that they’re planning to leave clinical medicine altogether because of it.

And hospital systems aren’t going out of their way to ease the situation. Private equity and mergers bring in money that should help expand staff and provide a better work environment.

On the contrary, doctors face heavier workloads than ever with no room for PTO. All to protect the bottom line for those at the top.

Private health systems chasing profit and the policy turmoil of declining reimbursement and Medicaid funding work together to create the perfect storm of doctors at their wits’ end. This month we saw exactly how that plays out in real life.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Nearly 150 unionized doctors at two Twin Cities hospitals went on strike, in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private sector hospital doctors in U.S. history.

This was not a spur-of-the-moment decision, but came after three years of bargaining that went nowhere. The health system had made $6 billion in 2025 revenue but was negotiating pay and sick time as if there were nothing left to give.

The cherry on top? A $26 billion merger behind closed doors.

In case you missed it: The Great Debate of Physician Unionization

Doctors represented by Doctors Council SEIU picketed outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and its Unity campus in Fridley for four days starting September 14, carrying signs reading “patients over profits.”

The union voted to unionize in 2023, sat through more than 60 bargaining sessions and authorized the strike with 90% support in July before giving the required 10 days’ notice.

Allina downplayed the disruption, stating that the union represents only about 10% of the physicians credentialed at both campuses and told the Minnesota Reformer that 37 union doctors crossed the picket line while 40 weren’t scheduled to work that week. Both campuses stayed open. The strike ran alongside a separate seven-day walkout by roughly 60 Allina hospice nurses.

Hospitalist Dr. Amber Galarowicz, on the union’s bargaining team, said that the fight isn’t just about pay. “We need to be able to stand up for ourselves,” she said.

Paid sick leave was likely the biggest factor. Minnesota law entitles full-time workers to six days a year but the doctors say they can’t take paid time off when they’re sick without dipping into vacation days.

Allina says its physicians already have paid leave and that it’s in compliance with state law. Never mind the fact that healthcare workers face a higher risk of getting ill.

“It’s become unsustainable for us to continue working like that,” said Dr. Alia Sharif, another bargaining team hospitalist.

Dr. John Wurst, who was part of the strike, said that doctors are also fighting to keep decision-making in physician hands, pointing to artificial intelligence tools that now weigh in on insurance billing as one example of ground already lost.

“We feel like we’re being excluded from decisions that affect the care of our patients,” Wurst said, adding that leaving physicians out of those calls means medical resources won’t end up allocated in a way that actually serves the community.

Cost of living adjustments have been part of the back and forth since last fall. This is amid rising inflation and fuel costs.

Coverage itself is also disputed. Because doctors often work across multiple Allina facilities, the two sides can’t agree on which physicians the union contract actually covers.

Doctors need to spend at least 20% of their time at Unity or Mercy to qualify for the bargaining unit but how that 20% gets calculated is still up in the air.

Apart from this local dispute, doctors across the nation are contending with policy changes that directly affects how much they earn.

Medicare’s 2026 physician fee schedule finalized a 2.5% “efficiency adjustment” that CMS says reflects services becoming easier to perform over time.

The policy applies to roughly 7,700 billing codes, including surgical procedures, diagnostic imaging interpretation, outpatient interventions, interventional pain management and orthopedic services.

Learn more: A Physician’s Guide to Medicare’s Specialty Care Changes — What’s Really Happening?

By law, Medicare physician payments have to stay budget neutral, meaning a raise for one group of doctors requires a cut somewhere else. Primary care physicians and time-based services keep the 2.5% increase Congress passed last year.

Specialists performing procedures have to watch that same increase get wiped out by the efficiency adjustment, and in some cases end up with a net cut once other changes are factored in.

The American Medical Association says that these changes will affect certain specialties more than others. More than a third of oncologists face cuts as steep as 20%. Over half of internists can expect reductions of 5% or more, and the same goes for 80% of infectious disease physicians.

One physician commented that as one of two infectious disease specialists in her region, the cuts would force her to refuse care to Medicare and Medicaid patients or simply retire.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 reconciliation law will cut federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 10 years, and 16 million people are projected to lose coverage through Medicaid or the ACA marketplace.

The layoffs stemming from these policy changes are no longer hypothetical. Back in June, Hennepin Healthcare in Minneapolis, in the same metro area as Allina’s Mercy and Unity campuses, announced roughly 100 layoffs this year and cut 100 inpatient beds, citing a $50 million shortfall tied directly to Medicaid revenue losses.

Trinity Health said it expects to lose $1.5 billion to “recent and future government policy changes.” Baptist Health in Arkansas laid off 150 employees, including 10 physicians, while shutting down its nephrology, pulmonary, oncology and infectious disease services.

Allina itself is telling employees that its economic decisions stem from “rising costs for drugs, supplies and labor, ongoing reimbursement pressures, increases in claim denials from insurance companies, and anticipated impacts from federal policy and reimbursement changes.”

Also read: What Physicians Should Know About the CMS Cut That Shaves Your Same-Day E/M Payment in Half

On top of all this is Allina’s proposed merger with Sutter Health, a California nonprofit, that would combine the two systems into a $26 billion operation spanning 39 hospitals across three states.

The merger is under review by the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office and opposed by labor unions who warn that consolidation tends to raise costs for patients while suppressing wage growth for the workers providing care.

Sharif said she doesn’t expect the union to block the deal but she’d like a community benefits agreement that shields against layoffs and service cuts, similar to one recently reached between the state and Sanford Health over its acquisition of a Robbinsdale hospital.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

For those who aren’t working at Mercy or Unity, this may feel abstract. It’s not.

Physician unionization has been on the rise because things that used to work, like individual negotiation, specialty societies lobbying CMS, and professional goodwill, keep losing to system-level budget decisions.

If you’re an employed physician, this deserves your attention. The same reimbursement structure and Medicaid cuts may come for whatever health system signs your paycheck.

Strikes make headlines because everyone has an opinion on them. Bureaucrats like to dismiss legitimate physician demands as unreasonable. But the jig is up, and the people are decrying the monopolization of our healthcare system.

The question is, what will it take to stop the consolidation machine?

Also read: A Physician’s Guide to Medicare’s Specialty Care Changes — What’s Really Happening?

Dr. Jordan Frey is a full-time practicing plastic surgeon and founder of The Prudent Plastic Surgeon, read by 20,000+ physicians. For five years, he has shared insights on personal finance, investing, career decisions, and financial independence while continuing to practice medicine.

A Physician on FIRE Partnership As part of our partnership, Physician on FIRE periodically shares select articles from The Prudent Plastic Surgeon with its readers.

About three months ago, I decided to actually give physician expert witness work a shot.

It was something that had been on my radar for a while. I knew other physicians did it. I knew it could be a lucrative side gig. And, at least on paper, it seemed to check a lot of the boxes that I look for in a physician side gig.

And three months later, after a bunch of cold outreach, a lot of conversations, a course on expert witness work, and several actual cases, including one involving a zebra, I figured it was a good time to share what I’ve learned so far.

The first thing I learned is that getting started in expert witness work is not particularly exciting.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

There was no moment where I signed up somewhere and cases suddenly started pouring in. Instead, there were a lot of emails, Zoom calls, and phone calls.

I reached out to lawyers. I talked to physicians who were already doing expert witness work. Plus I joined physician expert witness networks. I introduced myself, explained my expertise as a reconstructive plastic surgeon, sent my CV, and basically said, “If you ever need someone like me, keep me in mind.”

And I’ll admit, this felt a little uncomfortable. We aren’t really trained to market ourselves. For me, there was definitely a little bit of a feeling that I was shamelessly promoting myself. But eventually I started thinking about it differently.

We really are experts in our fields. And there are legal cases where an objective medical opinion can legitimately help a patient, a physician, or both. My job isn’t to advocate for whichever attorney happens to hire me. It’s to review the information and give an honest opinion based on my training and experience.

Once I reframed it that way, the outreach became a lot easier.

At the same time, I quickly realized that being an expert physician doesn’t automatically make you an expert witness. I understood the broad strokes. Review the medical records. Understand what happened. Form an opinion. Explain it.

But I didn’t really know how to structure a case review, what attorneys were looking for, how to write a report, how to create a fee schedule, or even how the business side of expert witness work typically operates.

That’s when I took Amy Fogelman’s High Rock Academy expert witness course. I found it incredibly helpful, particularly because it wasn’t just theoretical. There were actual resources and templates that I could use when cases started coming in, including report templates that I ultimately used for my first cases.

That preparation ended up being pretty well timed.

About six weeks after I really started pursuing this, I got my first case.

Ironically, my first case didn’t come from any of the cold outreach I had been doing. It came from a local physician friend who knew an attorney looking for someone with my expertise.

There’s probably an important lesson in there. You can send emails and join directories and market yourself all you want, but relationships still matter. The case involved aesthetic breast surgery and, to this point, has also been my most extensive case. There were a lot of records. There were depositions. And there were hours spent reviewing everything and figuring out exactly what happened.

Then I got on the phone with the attorneys.

This was probably the first time the work really clicked for me. They had very specific questions, and my job was essentially to do something that I already do every day as a physician: take a lot of complicated medical information, figure out what actually matters, form an opinion, and explain that opinion clearly.

That case is actually still ongoing, so there may be more work to come.

But after that first case, others started showing up.

I’ve now reviewed a handful of cases. Some have been relatively run-of-the-mill. And then there was the case involving an injury from a zebra.

I don’t remember that particular scenario coming up during plastic surgery residency.

But even that case reinforced what I’ve come to think is the biggest advantage of expert witness work for physicians: we already know how to do most of this. We spend our careers reviewing information, identifying what is relevant, synthesizing it, forming an assessment, and communicating that assessment to someone else. Sometimes that someone is a patient. Sometimes it’s another physician. And sometimes it’s an insurance company or hospital administrator.

In expert witness work, it happens to be an attorney.

That’s why, after only three months, I think this may be one of the better physician side gigs available. I used to list expert witness work as something I hadn’t personally done yet. Now I can at least start filling in that blank from experience.

Obviously, the income is part of the appeal.

One of the harder things when I started was figuring out what to charge. Talking to physicians who had done this before helped, as did seeing how others structured their fees.

I ultimately landed at $750 per hour with a five-hour minimum retainer.

So when I’m retained, I receive payment upfront for those first five hours. If the work goes beyond that, I bill additional time. I’ve had cases that exceeded the retainer and others that didn’t. But what matters to me isn’t just the hourly rate.

I’ve reviewed records early in the morning before my kids wake up. I’ve done work during their practices. And I’ve worked on cases in between operations while waiting for turnover.

That’s a meaningful distinction from clinical medicine, where income is about as directly tied to our physical presence as you can get. If I’m operating, seeing patients, or taking call, I can make money. If I’m not there, I generally don’t.

Expert witness work is still active income. I’m certainly not going to put it in the same category as the passive income streams I’ve built. But it’s active income on my terms.

Not every potential case turns into actual work.

This is particularly true with expert witness directories and referral companies. You may get contacted about a case, review some preliminary information, give a brief response, and then never hear anything else because the attorney chose someone else.

Do that enough times and it can become a real time suck. That’s one reason why, so far, I’ve preferred building direct relationships with attorneys.

And once you do get a case, my early impression is that the best marketing strategy is probably incredibly simple: Do a good job.

Be responsive. Be timely. You also need to be thorough without writing a 47-page treatise when three pages will do. Answer the questions being asked. Be easy to work with.

And most importantly, be honest. If your opinion isn’t what the attorney wants to hear, that’s still your opinion. The entire value of being an expert witness comes from being objective.

Do those things consistently and, I suspect, repeat business and referrals will follow.

There is one major part of expert witness work that I still haven’t experienced: Testifying.

I haven’t been deposed or testified at trial yet. So that’s an obvious blind spot in everything I’m saying here.

From talking to more experienced physician experts, my understanding is that most cases don’t ultimately involve courtroom testimony. A lot of the work is record review, conversations with attorneys, and written reports. Still, testimony is different. Being questioned by an opposing attorney while defending your opinions is not something we routinely do in clinical medicine.

When I eventually have that experience, I’ll write about it.

Physician expert witness work isn’t passive income. It’s scalable but requires effort, much in the same way that other physician side income streams can potentially require. And it isn’t something where you send a few emails and immediately have an overflowing pipeline of cases.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

But it does something that I think is incredibly valuable for physicians.

It takes expertise that we already spent years, really decades, developing and gives us another way to use it. And unexpectedly, I think it has already made me a better physician.

Reading cases retrospectively makes you think differently about documentation. It makes you think about how clinical decisions will look when someone reviews the chart a year later without any of the context you had in the moment. I’ve already found myself bringing some of those lessons back into my own practice.

A handful of hours of expert witness work can generate income comparable to working an extra clinical shift. Except I can do those hours before my kids wake up, at a practice, or whenever else they fit into my life.

And that gets back to the whole reason I’m pursuing financial freedom as a physician in the first place.

The goal isn’t just more money. It’s more control over my time. Three months in, expert witness work seems like a pretty good way to create a little more of both.

Visit the Iberia Plus website and locate their published off-peak date chart for your target route. Off-peak windows typically include January through March and October through November. Confirm your travel dates fall within the off-peak range before committing points.

Log into your Iberia Plus account and search for business class award flights on your target dates. Look for flights priced at 34,000 Avios one-way. If availability is not showing, try shifting dates by 1-2 days within the off-peak window.

Once you confirm availability, transfer points from Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, Citi ThankYou, or Marriott Bonvoy. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Allow 1-2 business days for others.

Complete the booking through the Iberia website using your Avios balance. Unlike many partner awards, Iberia off-peak bookings can be made entirely online without calling. Select your seat during the booking process.

Madrid is a natural hub for onward travel. Consider booking a separate low-cost carrier flight or Avios short-haul to Barcelona, Lisbon, or Seville. Iberia's short-haul Avios pricing is also excellent for intra-Europe connections.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

You're a great fit for this redemption if:

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.

When you’re ambitious, your mind keeps moving the finish line. Even when things are going well, you still hear the same thought: I should be doing more. You don’t always have the same energy.

A big context-dependent factor of your lifestyle is how, where, and when you spend money, and this can be influenced by whether or not you’re receiving a regularly scheduled paycheck. Studies show retirees are often overly frugal with their savings.

You read that right, we’re bringing the holiday spirit earlier this year with a discussion on how early is early enough to start planning for the holiday frenzy.

Now, Mariah Carey still has a couple months left before she’s summoned back to take over the radio, but you already know how this goes. Fall starts, and before you’ve finished raking a single leaf, Halloween candy is on clearance and you’re staring down two straight months of travel, shopping, gifts and family logistics.

Most people categorize this as an emotional gauntlet. It’s a time for family and mayhem, making new memories and reliving old ones.

For physicians, or any high earner really,  it’s also a financial trial. Having high income doesn’t magically make holiday spending a breeze. If anything, your wealth-building habits are put to their hardest test in November and December. It’s hard to be a spectator when everyone around you is spending like they’ve never heard of a budget.

Planning now, while the season still feels far off, is one of the ways you can get ahead of the season and its temptations.

The average American planned to spend around $890 per person last year on gifts, food, decorations and other seasonal costs, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual survey. That figure is the second highest in the survey’s 23-year history.

Last year, a Gallup survey found that consumers expected to spend $1,007 on gifts alone but that figure dropped to $778 by the time November actually arrived. That’s usually when the early enthusiasm comes face to face with the actual bank balance.

A family of four routinely spends $3,500 to $4,000 across the full season with travel and entertaining accounted for.

Those are reasonable numbers, some might even call them conservative. Which is fine as long as they align with the budget. But what happens when the spending exceeds what you had planned for?

In 2024, 36% of Americans took on new debt to cover holiday costs, averaging $1,181. Less than half (44%) of them expected to end up there. Average credit card balances aren’t slowing down either. According to Forbes, consumers, on average, owe more than $6,500.

Physicians aren’t immune to this. Heck, they might even be more vulnerable. High earners overspend for the same reason everyone else does. Decisions made in December, under time pressure, during the busiest clinical stretch of the year, have a way of getting out of hand.

Last year, Deloitte’s Holiday Retail Survey found that 57% of consumers expected the economy to weaken over the following six months, the most negative outlook Deloitte had recorded since it started tracking sentiment back in 1997.

Travel analyst Katy Nastro told Vox that domestic flights are typically best booked 3 to 7 months out, and international flights 4 to 10 months out. Booking your December trips in late September can be a gamechanger.

Rental cars follow the same logic. You don’t need to pay upfront, so reserving one now costs nothing and protects you from the price climb once inventory shrinks closer to the holidays.

Forbright Bank’s internal data on recurring deposits found that customers who automate savings consistently saw about 5 times the growth of those who don’t.

For a physician working full clinical hours, that invisible labor is a direct hit to the recovery time you need between shifts.

There’s also a well-documented cognitive cost to decision-making under pressure. Research on decision fatigue has repeatedly found that the quality of a person’s choices declines the more decisions they’ve already made that day.

Spreading holiday decisions across three months instead of cramming them into three weeks in December means less mental fatigue for the person who has to manage it all.

This is the most understandable objection, and also the one early planning actually solves.

I’m not suggesting you build a full itinerary this weekend. Take one task at a time like booking a flight or automating that recurring transfer. It can also be something as simple as asking family members what gifts they want this year.

These tasks are small enough that they should only take a couple of minutes but each one removes a decision you’d otherwise be making in December, when your schedule will be much worse.

Bankrate’s 2025 survey found that nearly half (49%) of holiday shoppers had already begun shopping before the end of October, which is consistent with prior years. You wouldn’t be the outlier you think you are. And getting the conversation going in the family group chat will help you mentally sort out a lot of the logistics before Halloween, even.

Many of us still believe that Black Friday is the best day to buy. That reputation doesn’t hold up well under scrutiny.

Accroding to Bankrate’s Ted Rossman, the deep discounts people associate with Black Friday now typically show up in early October instead.

WalletHub’s research has repeatedly found that 36% of items marketed as Black Friday deals offer no real savings compared to pricing in the weeks before.

Many of the products marketed heavily during the holiday season (toys and electronics in particular), actually get steeper discounts in December and January once retailers work through leftover inventory.

Waiting for a specific sale date isn’t the savings strategy many of us think it is.

To be fair to the skeptics, planning early isn’t free of trade-offs.

Locking in a flight or a purchase in September means giving up the chance that the price drops later. Booking early is a bet on certainty over optimization, which is reasonable for a flight with limited seats. Not so much for buying a gadget you could just as easily get on sale in January.

Ironically, the same early planning that is supposed to mitigate stress can sometimes morph into its own source of stress. You might start feeling more anxious the more you think about all the holiday stuff you still have to get done.

The planning process should be unintrusive enough that it doesn’t disrupt your current routine. Think of it like soup on the stove set to a slow simmer. Tasted and seasoned occasionally with some stirring here and there.

We tend to make the holidays all about the last two weeks of December. Which is honestly a small pay-off for months of planning but what if you could make the planning part of the fun?

Once your modified adjusted gross income crosses $200,000 single or $250,000 married filing jointly, the IRS tacks a 3.8% surtax onto your net investment income. Investing can feel exhausting when your work is already packed with tasks. Amid meetings, deadlines, family responsibilities, and day-to-day duties, it is unrealistic to allocate several hours of your day to market research.

The good part is that you don’t need to keep investing in research all the time to be a successful investor. All it takes is a small routine that keeps your knowledge current and gives you a sense of market developments without enslaving you to research.

The very beginning of it all is to set up a system that allows you to monitor major market events efficiently without drowning in too many online financial sites each morning.

Professionals use AlphaWire and similar platforms to access the latest news and details on individual companies quickly.

Using one main source of financial updates makes it much easier to see what is happening, and it significantly reduces the time you waste digging through different platforms.

This organized method of gathering stock market information can help you build and maintain your research routine over time.

One of the first things you can do is, for example, identify the companies that have been gaining traction, significant corporate news, movements in the stock markets, etc. You can then decide which of these topics merit further in-depth analysis.

It’s not about knowing everything or reading all the content out there. Set up a system that brings only the essential stuff to your attention so you can use your time effectively.

For many busy people, the 10 minutes or so they spend at the end of the workday isn’t enough to stay familiar with market developments.

Following the entire stock market at once is an easy way to waste time. In fact, one might think that a watchlist would be too limiting, but in reality, the opposite is true.

Your watchlist can include companies that you already own as well as companies that you are considering buying, a couple of their major rivals, and some key market indices related to the style you are using in your investment portfolio.

The watchlist would normally look like this:

The research boundaries have been limited in this way. When you ask yourself questions like, ‘What did the market do today?’ you will find answers that matter to the portfolio you follow by switching your question around.

https://unsplash.com/photos/stock-market-chart-displayed-on-laptop-screen-IrRbSND5EUc

It is a mistake to think you should complete all your daily research at once. You can divide the tasks across the week.

For example, Monday and Wednesday could be update days, while the other days could be for watchlist reviews and company reading sessions.

Differentiating the routine this way will help you stick with it. Dedicate a 30-minute session or a full-day activity during the weekend for conducting thorough research whenever needed.

Eventually, those short, regular sessions will give you such a solid grounding in your research that you will find it much easier to interpret and analyze any development.

Writing a journal of what you discover in the process of investing research is a good idea because it will be a great tool for your further study.

In fact, the simplest possible tools are often the most effective. You can use any plain text file or even a plain word processor file.

The information one could write about a company would include the company’s background, its revenue trends, the types of products or services it deals with, a description of its business model, its main products or services, its latest announcement, as well as industry trends it is involved in and any issue or question that you wish to get clarification on.

Your journals serve you as your personal library where you keep track of all your findings and research.

Later on, for instance, when you want to start anew on a topic, there should be no need for you to go back and read everything. You can remind yourself what you were thinking about and what you have learned before, and match it with what is going on now.

The idea behind investment research is to learn about and become familiar with the company or investment idea.

It may be a good practice to read about one stock repeatedly over time, but unless its changes are significant enough, you won’t make up your mind. That’s how it should be, because the more information you collect, the better your base understanding of the business, industry, and the company’s performance.

When you finally get a major piece of information about the company, you will immediately know the background without having to refer back to all your previous notes.

That is why retirement planning should not depend too heavily on a single age, a specific account balance, or a rigid view of the future.

For couples with a big age gap, the number of moving parts multiplies. Financial planners characterize the process as essentially having to knit together two different retirement trajectories and make it work for one family.

Sometimes we go completely down the personal finance rabbit hole. We use frugality as a weapon. We track every single cent we spend.
