When we talk about the cost-effectiveness of Systeme.io, we’re looking at a platform that offers a substantial suite of features without the hefty price tag that usually accompanies such versatility.

For starters, Systeme.io’s freemium model is a standout in the digital marketing space (click here to open a free account today). You can manage up to 2,000 contacts and create three sales funnels without spending a penny. This is a significant advantage for entrepreneurs and small businesses where every dollar counts.

To put this into perspective, let’s compare it with some industry counterparts. Platforms like ClickFunnels and Kartra, while offering robust functionalities, start their pricing at around $97 to $99 per month after their trial periods. This can be a steep investment for those just starting out.

In contrast, Systeme.io not only allows you to test the waters for free but also keeps the costs low even when you upgrade. Their paid plans, offering a broader range of features, start at less than $30 a month.

This pricing strategy makes advanced digital marketing tools accessible to a wider audience, breaking down the financial barriers that often hinder small businesses and startups.

The all-in-one nature of Systeme.io is its hallmark. It consolidates various marketing tools into one cohesive platform. This integration means you can manage email campaigns, build sales funnels, create websites, and even run affiliate programs without having to switch between different software. For many users, this integration simplifies the digital marketing process significantly, allowing for a more streamlined workflow.

However, it’s important to recognize that while Systeme.io covers a broad spectrum of functionalities, it may not offer the same depth as specialized standalone tools in each specific area.

For instance, while its email marketing capabilities are robust, they might not have the advanced features of a dedicated email marketing service.

Similarly, its website builder is competent for basic to intermediate needs, but it might not satisfy users looking for highly advanced web design features.

Systeme.io aims to be user-friendly, and for the most part, it achieves this goal. The interface is designed to be intuitive, especially for those who have basic familiarity with digital marketing tools. However, for complete beginners, there can be a learning curve.

The platform offers a range of tutorials and support materials, which are invaluable for new users. I’ve watched (and rewatched) several of these tutorials to lean how to use their software.

These resources are designed to help users navigate through the initial complexity and make the most out of the platform’s features.

Let’s get real about customization in Systeme.io. It’s got a decent selection of templates and the interface won’t make you pull your hair out, but if you’re looking to really dive deep into customization, you might hit a wall.

For those who have grand visions of a highly unique and tailored digital presence, Systeme.io can feel a bit like playing with kid gloves. It’s great for getting you up and running, but for the more ambitious or specific design needs, it’s not quite the creative playground you might be looking for.

Now, onto scalability. Systeme.io is like that compact car that’s perfect for city driving but struggles a bit on the open highway. For small businesses or solo entrepreneurs just starting out, it’s a match made in heaven. But as your business grows and your needs become more complex, Systeme.io might start to feel a bit cramped.

This is especially true for larger businesses or those niche ventures that need more than just the basics. As you scale up, you might find yourself needing more sophisticated tools and features that Systeme.io doesn’t offer.

Plus, when it comes to playing nice with other tools or services you might be using, Systeme.io isn’t always the most cooperative. It works well within its own confines but doesn’t always reach out to others easily.

When compared to competitors, Systeme.io’s pricing is highly competitive. For instance, platforms like ClickFunnels offer powerful functionality but at a higher cost, typically starting at around $100 per month after a free trial. This can be a significant investment, especially for new entrepreneurs or small businesses.

In contrast, Systeme.io’s paid plans, which provide access to a broader range of features, are more affordable, starting at less than $30 a month.

ClickFunnels, on the other hand, is more expensive but offers highly customizable funnel-building capabilities.

User reviews and testimonials play a crucial role in understanding the real-world effectiveness of Systeme.io. Many users have shared success stories, highlighting how the platform has helped them streamline their marketing efforts and grow their businesses.

Upon reviewing their Trustpilot account, you can see the experience with Systeme.io is remarkable. Currently, there are 3,635 reviews with an average rating of 4.9. That is outstanding!

However, it’s also important to consider critiques and common issues raised by users. Some have pointed out the limitations in customization and scalability, as mentioned earlier. These critiques are valuable for potential users to set realistic expectations and for the platform’s developers to identify areas for improvement.

In essence, while Systeme.io is a fantastic starting point for new online businesses, offering a solid foundation and easy-to-use tools, it’s not the endgame for everyone.

As your business evolves, you might outgrow its capabilities and start looking for something that offers a bit more room to stretch your entrepreneurial legs.

It’s a great launchpad, but for those on a path to rapid growth or with highly specific needs, keep in mind that you might need to eventually graduate to more advanced tools.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins

Here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

Virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart currently prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:

For a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

Virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Do NOT start at Virgin Atlantic's website — their search tool for partner awards is limited. Instead, go directly to delta.com and search for your desired route (e.g., JFK → LAX) in the date range you're targeting. Select "Use miles" as your payment method and filter by Business class. You're not booking here — you're prospecting.

What you're looking for: Delta One availability showing in the results. When you see it, note the exact flight number, date, and departure time. Delta.com will show you the SkyMiles price (which will be high under dynamic pricing), but ignore that number entirely. You just need to confirm the seat exists.

You need 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person. Before transferring anything, confirm which flexible points currency you're working with:

All transfer at 1:1 instantly. If you're using Marriott Bonvoy points, the ratio is 3:1 (so 150,000 Bonvoy points = 50,000 Flying Club miles), and transfers take 1–5 days.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific flight, transfer your points. Use the transfer portal within your credit card program's website (Chase, Amex, Citi, or Bilt). You'll need your Flying Club membership number — create a free account at virginatlantic.com/us/en/flying-club if you don't have one.

For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers: miles appear instantly in your Flying Club account. Confirm the balance before proceeding.

Critical warning: Do not transfer points until you've verbally confirmed availability with a Virgin Atlantic agent (Step 4). Points transfers are irreversible.

This is a phone booking, not an online booking. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at 1-800-365-9500. Have your flight details ready:

Ask the agent to confirm that Delta One award availability exists on your chosen flight before you transfer points. If they confirm it, then transfer and call back — or ask to be placed on a brief hold while you complete the transfer (instant transfers make this possible).

Once your miles are transferred and the agent has confirmed availability, they'll complete the booking. You'll pay only standard carrier taxes and fees — expect roughly $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. route. You'll receive a Virgin Atlantic booking confirmation, but your ticket will show Delta as the operating carrier.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. For the best seat selection and availability, aim to search within that window as early as possible.

Delta SkyMiles uses fully dynamic pricing with no published award chart, meaning business class awards can range from 80,000 to 500,000 SkyMiles for the same route depending on demand. Virgin Atlantic, as a Delta joint venture partner, maintains a fixed award chart for Delta-operated flights — creating a massive pricing arbitrage. A JFK-to-London Delta One Suite that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles can often be booked through Virgin for 47,500 Flying Club miles. Both programs see the same award inventory, but Virgin prices it using their distance-based chart instead of Delta's demand-based algorithm. Since Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club accepts 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, you can earn these miles through credit card spending without ever flying Virgin Atlantic.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers become concrete.

The Route: New York JFK → Los Angeles LAX The Aircraft: Airbus A350-900 The Cabin: Delta One Suites

Pull up Delta.com on a typical travel date and you'll find Delta One Suites on this route priced anywhere from $2,500 for a off-peak weekday to $5,000–$6,000 during peak summer weekends or holiday travel. Let's use a realistic midpoint of $3,500 — a completely standard price for business class on one of America's most competitive routes.

If you earned those 50,000 points via a Chase Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus (currently 60,000 points) and some organic spend, your real cost to acquire the points was a small fraction of the flight's retail value.

You check in at JFK's Terminal 4 with Delta status access or a Priority Pass card in hand, clearing into the Delta Sky Club or the premium Centurion Lounge (if you carry the Amex Platinum). Then you board the A350-900 and find your suite.

The five-hour flight from New York to Los Angeles becomes an experience rather than a commute. You arrive rested, full, and having spent roughly $11 out of pocket on a seat your fellow passengers paid $3,500 for. That gap — that's the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in action.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. Delta One availability on high-demand routes like JFK–LAX is not unlimited — it's released in waves and often fills quickly for peak dates. Set a calendar reminder to search exactly 331 days before your target travel date. This is especially important for holiday travel, summer weekends, and any dates where you have a hard deadline.

Since transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are instant, you can do a same-call transfer — confirm availability with the agent, ask them to hold for a moment, transfer your points in a separate browser tab, and confirm with the agent that the miles have landed. This eliminates the risk of availability disappearing between your transfer and your booking attempt.

While this sweet spot is available year-round, Delta One availability is generally better on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday departures when leisure demand is lower. If your travel dates are flexible, searching across a week of dates will often surface better availability on midweek flights.

Virgin Atlantic's award chart has high fuel surcharges on Virgin Atlantic-operated flights. This guide is specifically about Delta-operated flights. Never confuse the two. When you call to book, confirm the operating carrier is Delta. The surcharge-free benefit applies only to partner awards.

Points transfers are irreversible. A common and painful mistake is transferring points to Flying Club only to discover the specific flight you wanted has no award availability. Always confirm availability verbally with a Flying Club agent before initiating any transfer.

The most efficient path to 50,000 points is a single credit card welcome bonus. The Chase Sapphire Preferred or Chase Sapphire Reserve both offer welcome bonuses that can fully fund this redemption — and both transfer to Virgin Atlantic at 1:1 instantly. Alternatively, the Amex Gold Card or Platinum Card welcome bonuses work equally well via Amex's instant transfer path.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A simple fix: make a small earning transaction (even a hotel stay or car rental through their partners) at least once every three years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want a genuinely luxurious experience on one of America's premier transcontinental routes and are comfortable with a moderate amount of booking complexity — primarily a phone call to Virgin Atlantic.

Minimum points needed: 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person (100,000 for two). These are most efficiently sourced via a single credit card welcome bonus.

For the FI-minded traveler who has earned a moderate points balance and wants to experience premium cabin travel on a meaningful domestic route, this is a standout use of currency. The 5–12 CPP range makes it one of the most efficient domestic business class redemptions available.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — not because any individual step is technically complex, but because it requires coordinating two separate systems (Delta.com for availability searching and Virgin Atlantic by phone for booking) and making an irreversible transfer decision under some time pressure. **What makes it moderately challenging:** 1. **Availability is the main hurdle.** Delta One award inventory released to partners is limited, particularly on peak dates. You won't always find seats when you want them, and the 331-day booking window means planning further ahead than most travelers are accustomed to. 2. **The booking requires a phone call.** There's no self-service online booking for Virgin Atlantic partner awards. Some travelers find this intimidating; in practice, Flying Club agents are helpful and accustomed to partner award bookings. 3. **The transfer-before-booking sequence requires discipline.** The rule is: confirm first, transfer second. Getting that order wrong is an expensive mistake. **Three tips to make this easier:** - **Use Delta.com as your search engine.** It shows real-time award availability far more reliably than third-party tools for Delta-operated flights. - **Call Virgin Atlantic during off-peak hours** (early morning Eastern time tends to mean shorter hold times and more patient agents). - **Have your flight details written down** before you call — flight number, date, origin, destination, and Flying Club number. A prepared caller gets a faster, smoother booking. If you've ever transferred points to an airline program and called to book an award, this process will feel completely familiar. If this is your first partner award booking, treat it as a learning experience — the 5–12 CPP reward on the other side is well worth one phone call.

Log into your Delta SkyMiles account and search for one-way business class (Delta One) award flights. Filter for nonstop flights on the A350-900, which is the aircraft with Delta One Suites. Note the dates that show availability — this is the same inventory Virgin can book.

If you do not already have a Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, create one at virginatlantic.com. You need an active account to receive transferred miles and to reference when calling to book.

Transfer the required miles from your preferred partner: Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant transfer), Amex Membership Rewards (typically 1-2 business days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant to 24 hours), or Bilt (1-2 days). Always confirm availability before transferring.

Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at their US number. Provide the specific flight number, date, and route you found on delta.com. The agent will search for the same availability and quote the mileage cost from Virgin's fixed award chart. Confirm the booking and pay taxes and fees.

Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart prices Delta One flights based on distance. Transatlantic routes (US to Europe) typically cost 47,500 to 60,000 Virgin miles one-way in business class. Transpacific routes cost more, around 60,000 to 80,000 miles. Compare this to Delta SkyMiles, which can charge 200,000 to 500,000 miles for the same seats.

No. As of 2026, Virgin Atlantic does not support online booking for Delta partner awards. You must call Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club phone line to book. Search for availability on delta.com first, then call with the specific flight details. The call typically takes 10-15 minutes.

Delta One is the business class cabin available on multiple aircraft types with lie-flat seats but no closing door. Delta One Suites are only on the A350-900 and feature a fully enclosed suite with a closing door, a wider seat, and a more private experience. When booking, verify the aircraft type is A350-900 to ensure you get the Suite product.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Virgin Atlantic are instant. Citi ThankYou points are also fast, typically completing within minutes to 24 hours. Amex Membership Rewards and Bilt usually take 1-2 business days. Capital One transfers take 1-2 days as well. If you find availability and need to book quickly, Chase is the best source.

Booking Delta One Suites through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is the definitive workaround for Delta's punishing dynamic pricing. Paying 50,000 transferable points for a seat that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles is one of the largest arbitrage opportunities in travel rewards. The fully enclosed suite with a closing door is the best international business class product any US carrier offers. Yes, you need to call to book — but that 15-minute phone call saves you 300,000 miles. Build your transferable points balances with Chase, Amex, or Bilt, search delta.com for A350 availability, and let Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart do the rest.

Online banking is like traditional banking, except you conduct transactions online or at an ATM.

Some banks allow you to deposit cash at local retailers, but be careful because there are sometimes fees.

The nice thing about online banking is you can bank 24/7; you don’t have to worry about traditional bank hours.

You can electronically transfer funds, deposit checks with the bank’s mobile app, and use a bank’s unique features.

If you’re weary of banking online, check out the advantages you can take advantage of:

So what’s the difference between online and traditional banking?

It comes down to where you bank, either from your couch or the bank teller’s counter.

Physical banks have tellers, but you can only bank during their hours and must visit the bank in person. However, many traditional banks offer online services today, too.

Online banking offers the same services, but from your home or anywhere you have an internet connection.

The toughest thing about online banking is how you deposit or withdraw cash. Some of the best online banks have a robust ATM network that allows you to handle cash, but not all do, so always find out first.

Always choose an FDIC-insured online bank that uses safety features, such as two-factor authentication and bank-level encryption.

If a bank is FDIC-insured, your funds are protected up to $250,000 per depositor should the bank close.

When choosing an online bank, consider these factors:

As you probably guessed, you can open an online bank account online.

You’ll need basic information such as your name, address, birth date, and Social Security number. You must also upload a government-issued ID to prove your identity.

Once you open the account, you’ll link an external account to fund it, or you may be able to deposit cash at a local ATM.

We use several key factors to evaluate and find the best online banks, including the following:

Still, have questions about online banks and managing money online? We have answers.

Online bank rates, yields, and fees are subject to change at banks’ discretion. Check their websites or call customer service for up-to-date information about specific accounts and bank policies.

Online banks are generally more affordable than traditional banks. They’re less likely to charge monthly maintenance fees on checking and savings accounts, and many have fewer hidden fees, too.

That also depends on the individual bank, but many online accounts feature higher yields than traditional banks.

Online banks have less overhead than traditional banks, and they don’t need to pay to keep big, centrally located branches open or pay people to work at them. Their operations are more efficient, which allows them to pass the savings on to customers via higher rates and lower fees.

It depends on the bank and its website or app structure, but it’s usually straightforward. In fact, with an online-only bank, enrollment is usually automatic. You don’t have to complete a separate application or even click a button to activate your account.

However, you must create a unique username and password to get started. You may be asked to do this as part of the initial application process or once your account is approved. You’ll also need to link at least one external funding source to transfer money into your account.

Some online banks offer home loans (mortgages) and other credit products. These banks are larger online banks with high name recognition, like Ally Bank and Capital One Bank. Look for a “Mortgages” or “Home Loans” tab on the homepage or your account dashboard.

Be aware that some online banks outsource mortgage origination to other companies. In other words, if you apply for a mortgage through your bank, your loan officer might work for someone else. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but it could mean a different level or style of service than you’re used to.

And don’t expect your online bank to offer better mortgage rates than other lenders. The mortgage loan business is highly competitive, and direct lenders with even lower overhead may be able to undercut online banks.

The best online banks on this list offer a great combination of FDIC-insured banking products, solid yields, open access, and helpful customer service.

Before choosing one, look closely at the features that set it apart from the competition: rewards checking, flexible withdrawal terms for CDs, particularly high account yields, a socially responsible corporate philosophy, and so on.

A high-yield savings account offers a higher interest rate compared to traditional savings accounts.

These accounts are typically offered by online banks or credit unions, and they provide an opportunity for individuals to grow their savings more quickly.

The competitive rates are the main feature that sets high-yield savings accounts apart from regular savings accounts.

With a high-yield savings account, you can earn more money on your savings over time, allowing your funds to grow at a faster rate. This can be especially beneficial if you’re looking to save for a specific financial goal, such as a down payment on a house or an emergency fund.

However, it’s important to note that high-yield savings accounts may have limitations compared to traditional savings accounts, like minimum balance requirements or withdrawal limits.

It’s important to research and compare different high-yield savings account options to find the one that best suits your needs and financial goals. If you do that, a high-yield savings account can be a useful tool to help you save more effectively and achieve your financial objectives.

Before you open an account, take a look at the benefits and drawbacks of a HYSA.

HYSAs aren’t the only way for savers to accelerate their financial goals. As you compare account options, see if your bank offers some of the following account types:

When you’re choosing a high-yield savings account, there are several key factors to consider.

To help you make the most informed decision, here’s a detailed list of what to look for:

By keeping these factors in mind, you can find a high-yield savings account that suits your needs and helps you grow your savings efficiently.

Here’s how we select the Best High-Yield Savings Accounts.

Our editorial team evaluates high-yield savings accounts on several key metrics that can make or break your experience as an account holder.

For each metric, we select the account that surpasses all other competitors — giving you the confidence you need to choose the product that works best for you.

Your savings account’s yield is a function of its interest rate and compounding frequency.

Compounding frequency describes how often your account adds the interest it’s earned to the original (principal) balance. The higher the compounding frequency, the longer each extra bit of interest has to earn interest on itself.

For example, imagine two seemingly identical savings accounts. Both earn 0.50% interest. The only difference: Account A compounds annually and Account B compounds daily.

You seed both accounts with $10,000 and make no further deposits. The interest rate remains level at 0.50%. By Year 10, how much bigger is Account B’s balance?

A whopping $1.31, that’s how much. After accounting for inflation, the difference is even smaller.

Federal deposit insurance (FDIC coverage) protects savings balances held with member FDIC institutions up to at least $250,000. That protection kicks in if the member bank fails.

Always ensure your bank is FDIC-insured. Otherwise, there’s no guarantee you’ll get your money back if it closes its doors.

FDIC insurance doesn’t cover everything that can go wrong at your bank. It might not reimburse you if your account is hacked and drained without your consent or if you fall victim to a financial scam.

Some banks continue to charge excess withdrawal fees. But a growing number of financial institutions now choose to waive them.

That’s because of a long-overdue change to a Federal Reserve bylaw known as Regulation D (Reg D). For years, Reg D limited withdrawals or payments from savings and money market accounts to six per statement period.

In April 2020, the Federal Reserve announced that deposit institutions were no longer bound by the strict monthly withdrawal limit.

FDIC-insured high-yield savings accounts are completely safe, insuring your funds for up to $250,000, with some banks offering even higher levels of protection.

The best high-yield savings accounts also take extensive measures to protect your private information

Choosing a high-yield savings account can feel overwhelming, so take a step back before you make your pick and consider which factors matter most to you.

Often, the decision process begins and ends with yield. If that’s the case for you, choose the highest-yielding savings account you can find.

Try not to overthink it. Opening a savings account isn’t something to be done lightly, but it’s also not as big a deal as buying a car or house. You can always open another one if you decide your first choice wasn’t the right one.

#8580. Set Your FSA Contribution From Last Year’s Medical Bills – Not the Maximum

At open enrollment, base your health flexible spending account (FSA) contribution on last year’s costs that will repeat, like prescriptions, copays, glasses, and dental work. The money you put in skips federal income and payroll taxes, but what’s left at the plan’s deadline is lost, apart from any small carryover. Elect only what you’re sure to spend.

Whatever you elect holds for the whole plan year. You can change it only after a life event your plan recognizes, such as a marriage, birth, or adoption.

The full amount is available on the plan’s first day, before it has come out of your pay, so you can cover a big bill early in the plan year.

The catch is the deadline. Money you haven’t spent by the end of the plan year is lost. Your plan may add a grace period of up to two and a half months to spend it, or let a small amount carry over to the next year, but not both. So the right contribution is what you’re sure to spend, not the IRS’s yearly maximum, unless you’re certain to spend that much.

Start with last year’s out-of-pocket costs, which your insurer’s claims history and your pharmacy receipts show. Then count the costs you know you’ll have next year:

Leave out one-time bills, such as urgent care for a sprain. Say you’re in the 22% federal tax bracket, pay the standard 7.65% Social Security and Medicare tax, and those costs total $1,900. Electing $1,800 instead of $1,900 leaves a $100 cushion in case your costs drop and saves you $396 in federal income tax plus about $138 in Social Security and Medicare tax.

If you’ll have a health savings account, a regular health FSA would stop your contributions to it, but a limited-purpose FSA for dental and vision care works alongside one. Child care goes in a separate dependent care FSA.

Pull those records before your enrollment window closes, add up the costs you know are coming, and elect a little under the total. Near the end of the plan year, check your balance and spend what’s left before the deadline on care you’d buy anyway.

Good credit in your home country can still count in the U.S. If home is the United Kingdom or Canada, Chase can use your credit history there. If you’ve held a card from American Express itself abroad for at least three months, Amex can use that account. Check both before you settle for a card that needs a deposit.

A U.S. credit file starts empty, however long your record abroad. So a newcomer with years of on-time payments looks like a first-time borrower, the kind who usually starts on a secured card, backed by a cash deposit.

Chase can use the credit history you built in the U.K. or Canada, through Nova Credit, a company that converts a foreign credit report into a U.S.-style report and score. For now, Chase does this only on the Freedom Unlimited and the Freedom Flex.

American Express uses a different record, the Amex card you hold in another country. If Amex itself issued that card, not a partner bank, you’re its main cardholder, and you’ve had it at least three months, Amex may base its decision on that account’s history. Keep it open and in good standing until you apply, or apply within three months of closing it. You can apply for one U.S. card this way, and for more once you’ve built U.S. credit.

On Chase’s application, check the box asking Chase to consider your international credit history, then follow any instructions Chase sends for your report. For Amex, pick the U.S. American Express card you want, click the Already a Card Member link on its application, and enter your current account number, U.S. home address, and U.S. phone number. Amex takes passport details if you don’t have a Social Security number yet.

Say a nurse moves from Canada with a Social Security number, a U.S. address, and eight years of on-time payments on her Canadian report. Checking the box on a Freedom Unlimited application can get her a regular card, no deposit needed. A colleague with the same record who skips the box spends her first year on a secured card.

Newcomers who fit neither route can open a Chase checking or savings account with at least $250, then apply for the Freedom Rise, a Chase card for people new to credit. Chase says that balance improves your approval odds, and a secured card stays your backup.

## Flying Business Class Across Two Continents for the Price of One Imagine settling into a fully flat bed on a Boeing 787-9 somewhere over the Pacific, a warm towel in your hand, Japan behind you and Singapore ahead. You've already spent three days eating ramen in Tokyo — a stopover you added to your award ticket for a mere 5,000 extra points. This isn't a once-in-a-lifetime splurge. This is what the ChooseFI community calls a **nearly free** trip, engineered through one of the most underappreciated sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The Air Canada Aeroplan stopover rule is genuinely one of the last great loopholes in loyalty travel. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop: a business class flight from Toronto to Singapore — routed through Tokyo with a multi-day stopover — retails for **$8,000 to $10,000 in cash**. You can book that same itinerary for **70,000 Aeroplan points** (plus 5,000 for the stopover, so 75,000 total). At a conservative cash value of $8,000, you're extracting **10.7 cents per point** — more than double what most programs offer, and squarely within Aeroplan's documented range of **5.7 to 14.3 cents per point**. To put that in FI terms: if you value your points at even the low end of that range — 5.7 cents per point — 75,000 Aeroplan points are worth **$4,275 in travel**. At the high end, you're looking at **$10,725**. That's a portfolio-level return on the credit card spending and transfer partners you've already been accumulating. What makes this feel different from other premium redemptions is the *shape* of the trip itself. You're not just flying business class — you're building a mini round-the-world itinerary. Tokyo and Singapore in the same award ticket. Two of the world's great cities. Two business class flights. One redemption. The inefficiency here isn't accidental — it's baked into how Aeroplan prices stopovers at a flat 5,000 miles, regardless of where you stop. The program is essentially inviting you to stack experiences on a single award, and the ChooseFI community is the group paying close enough attention to accept that invitation.

The core insight is this: Air Canada Aeroplan uses a fixed partner award chart for Star Alliance flights, and it prices stopovers at a flat 5,000-mile premium regardless of routing complexity. That single policy decision transforms a standard business class award into a multi-destination adventure at a fraction of the combined retail cost.

Here's the mechanism. When Aeroplan relaunched in 2020, it did something most programs had abandoned years earlier: it kept a fixed-rate award chart for partner airlines. While programs like United MileagePlus moved to fully dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate with demand — Aeroplan locked in predictable rates for Star Alliance partners. The YYZ to SIN corridor in business class sits at a rate that reflects the geography, not the current demand spike or revenue management algorithm. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community can systematically exploit.

Layer on top of that the stopover rule: Aeroplan allows one free stopover on one-way partner awards for just 5,000 additional miles. A stopover is defined as a connection of more than 24 hours. So your Toronto → Tokyo → Singapore routing becomes a Toronto → Tokyo (stopover 3 days) → Singapore itinerary, all on one award ticket, for 75,000 points total. You've essentially purchased two separate international business class flights for the price of one, plus a nominal surcharge.

The other critical piece: Aeroplan charges zero fuel surcharges on partner awards. This was a deliberate policy decision in the 2020 relaunch and it's a massive advantage. Programs like British Airways Avios and Singapore KrisFlyer can add $500–$1,500 in surcharges to long-haul business class awards. With Aeroplan, you pay government taxes only — typically $50–$150 on most itineraries.

You don't need to fly Air Canada or hold an Air Canada credit card to access this. Aeroplan accepts transfers from several major flexible currency programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is your best friend here because transfers are instant, which matters when you're racing to book a specific award seat before someone else claims it. If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, your UR points can become Aeroplan points in seconds.

The booking window is 355 days out, which gives you nearly a full year of planning runway — a significant advantage for families coordinating schedules or travelers targeting peak periods in Tokyo or Singapore. Partner award availability on Aeroplan is generally solid for the Star Alliance network, with business class seats on ANA, Japan Airlines (where applicable), and Singapore Airlines routes opening up regularly. Availability scores a 4 out of 5 for this sweet spot, which reflects genuine accessibility rather than theoretical possibility.

Never transfer points until you have confirmed, bookable award space in hand. Go to aeroplan.com and use the flight search tool. Select "Business" class, enter your origin and destination (e.g., Toronto YYZ to Singapore SIN), and search for one-way awards. Aeroplan's search engine will show you available partner space directly — you don't need a separate search on partner airline websites, though checking ana.co.jp or singaporeair.com for business class availability can help you triangulate what's open before logging into Aeroplan.

Look for awards showing Star Alliance partner carriers (ANA, Singapore Airlines, and others depending on routing). The system will display the points cost and any routing options. Aeroplan's booking window opens 355 days in advance, so set a calendar reminder to search the moment your target travel window becomes available.

Once you've found an outbound flight you like (e.g., Toronto → Tokyo), call Aeroplan at 1-800-361-5373 or use the online multi-city search to add a stopover at your midpoint city. A stopover is any connection exceeding 24 hours. The system will add 5,000 points to your base award cost. Confirm the full itinerary shows both the Tokyo stopover segment and the onward Tokyo → Singapore flight in the cabin class you want.

Note: Online booking for complex multi-city awards with stopovers sometimes requires a phone call to complete. Budget 30–45 minutes for the call and have your routing clearly written out before you dial.

Determine which flexible currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards, transfer to Aeroplan first — it's instant. Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners," select Air Canada Aeroplan, and complete the transfer. Points appear in your Aeroplan account immediately.

If using Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One, or Bilt, initiate the transfer and expect a 1–2 day processing window. Have your Aeroplan member number ready. Do NOT transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1.

Once your points land in your Aeroplan account, return to aeroplan.com and complete the booking within the same browser session if possible. Pay the government taxes and fees with a credit card that earns rewards on travel purchases. Taxes on a routing like YYZ → NRT → SIN are typically in the $100–$200 range — no fuel surcharges.

After booking, download or screenshot your itinerary confirmation. Verify the cabin class on each segment. Check in on the Aeroplan website 24 hours before each flight and confirm your seat assignments. For the stopover city, you are responsible for your own accommodation — budget accordingly, and consider this the best "forced layover" you'll ever take.

A stopover is a deliberate break in your journey at a connecting city, where you stay for more than 24 hours before continuing to your final destination. Most loyalty programs treat stopovers as separate tickets, requiring you to pay miles for each segment independently. Aeroplan breaks this convention by allowing one free stopover on one-way awards, meaning your connecting city becomes a bonus destination at zero additional mileage cost. For example, a flight from New York to Tokyo with a 5-day stopover in Istanbul costs the same 75,000 Aeroplan points as flying directly — but you get to explore Istanbul for nearly a week as part of the trip. The stopover must be at a connection point that makes geographic sense for your routing, but with 26+ Star Alliance airlines and hundreds of hub cities, the options are vast.

Let's build out a specific redemption so the math becomes undeniable.

The Itinerary: You depart Toronto Pearson (YYZ) on an ANA Boeing 787-9 bound for Tokyo Narita (NRT). You've built in a 3-day stopover in Tokyo — enough time for a morning at Tsukiji, an evening in Shinjuku, and a day trip to Nikko. Then you board a Singapore Airlines flight from NRT to Singapore Changi (SIN) in Business Class.

The Cash Price: A business class itinerary covering this exact routing — YYZ to NRT to SIN — retails in the range of $8,000 to $10,000, depending on season and carrier. Booking two separate one-way tickets (YYZ-NRT and NRT-SIN) in business class would easily exceed that, often landing closer to $10,000–$12,000 combined.

The Points Cost: 70,000 Aeroplan points for the base award + 5,000 for the stopover = 75,000 points total, plus approximately $120–$180 in government taxes. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP Calculation: At a midpoint cash value of $9,000, your 75,000 points are generating 12 cents per point. Even at the conservative $8,000 end, you're at 10.7 cents per point — well within the documented 5.7–14.3 cent range and significantly above the ChooseFI rule of thumb of 2 cents per point for most redemptions.

On the ANA 787-9 YYZ–NRT segment, you're in ANA's Business Staggered seat — a fully flat bed with direct aisle access, Japanese hospitality, and one of the best business class dining experiences in the sky. The Tokyo stopover is yours to explore however you like. Then Singapore Airlines' Business Class on the NRT–SIN leg offers its own benchmark product — a refined seat, excellent service, and arrival into Changi, consistently ranked the world's best airport.

You've visited two of Asia's most celebrated cities, flown on two world-class airlines, slept flat across the Pacific, and your out-of-pocket cash cost was under $200. That is the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in its purest form.

Tokyo in cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and autumn foliage season (November) books up incredibly fast — even in business class. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 355 days before your target departure and search the moment Aeroplan's window opens. Partner award space on popular routes gets claimed quickly.

Because Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Aeroplan instantly, you can hold an award seat without pre-positioning points in your account. Find the space first, then transfer exactly what you need. This is a significant tactical advantage over programs that require 2–5 day transfer windows.

Aeroplan allows open jaw routing. You can fly INTO Tokyo and OUT of Singapore on separate awards, pairing this business class redemption with a separate economy or business award home. Build your Southeast Asia trip so you land in one city and depart from another — no backtracking, better geography, same award pricing framework.

This is the single most common mistake in all of travel rewards. If you transfer 75,000 Chase UR to Aeroplan and then discover the award space disappeared, you cannot transfer back. Chase points are gone. Confirm bookable space first, transfer second, book third.

Marriott transfers to Aeroplan at a 3:1 ratio — meaning you need 225,000 Marriott points to generate 75,000 Aeroplan points. That's an extraordinarily poor ratio for this redemption. Use Chase, Amex, Capital One, or Bilt instead.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve earns 3x on travel and dining. The Amex Platinum earns 5x on flights booked directly. Build your Aeroplan balance through the transfer partners rather than flying Air Canada itself — the flexibility is far more valuable.

Unlike many programs that expire your miles after 12–18 months of inactivity, Aeroplan points never expire. This means you can accumulate slowly and deliberately — a natural fit for the FI community's patient, systematic approach to building travel rewards balances.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers with a genuine interest in Asia — specifically anyone who has ever dreamed of Japan and Southeast Asia in the same trip without paying for two separate premium tickets. If your travel bucket list includes Tokyo and Singapore in the same itinerary, this is the single most efficient way to get there in business class.

Minimum points needed: ~75,000 Aeroplan points (70,000 base + 5,000 stopover). Build this through Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, or Bilt transfers.

For the FI-minded traveler, this is a high-ROI, low-cash-cost adventure that fits perfectly into a strategy of saving aggressively while experiencing the world nearly free.

## Why This Is Rated Moderate — And How to Handle It This sweet spot earns a **moderate difficulty** rating — not because the math is complicated, but because the booking process has more moving parts than a simple domestic award. **What makes it moderate:** 1. **Complex routing with a stopover** — Aeroplan's online tool doesn't always handle multi-city stopover bookings cleanly. You may need to call Aeroplan to finalize the itinerary, which adds a step and requires you to have your routing clearly planned before you dial. 2. **Partner award availability** — You're booking seats on ANA, Singapore Airlines, or other Star Alliance carriers, not Air Canada. Partner space is real and accessible (this scores a 4/5 for availability), but it requires searching specifically for it on aeroplan.com and sometimes triangulating with partner airline websites. 3. **Points transfer timing** — You need points in your Aeroplan account before completing the booking, which means coordinating a transfer after confirming space exists. Chase's instant transfer largely solves this problem. **Three tips to make it manageable:** - **Use aeroplan.com's multi-city search first** to understand what routing options exist before calling. Come to any phone call with a primary and backup itinerary already researched. - **Book 6–12 months out** using the 355-day window. More availability, more flexibility, less stress. - **Do one transfer before you need to** — move a small amount of points to Aeroplan just to practice the process and verify your accounts are linked. If you've successfully booked a domestic business class award before, this is a natural next step. The complexity is manageable, and the reward — business class across two ocean crossings with a Tokyo stopover — is absolutely worth the extra 45 minutes of work.

Identify your final destination and choose a stopover city that lies along a logical routing. Popular stopover cities include Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), Tokyo (ANA hub), Frankfurt (Lufthansa hub), and Zurich (Swiss hub). The stopover city must be a connection point that Aeroplan considers valid for your route.

On aircanada.com, use the multi-city search option. Enter your origin to the stopover city as the first segment, and the stopover city to your final destination as the second segment. Set business class and search. The system will show you combined availability and pricing with the stopover included.

Once you confirm availability, transfer the required points from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant to 24 hours), Amex Membership Rewards (1-3 days), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Transfer only after confirming both segments have availability.

Follow the booking flow on aircanada.com, selecting both segments. The system will recognize the stopover and price it as a single one-way award. Confirm the total mileage cost matches the one-way rate for your destination — the stopover should add zero additional miles.

With up to 45 days at your stopover city, plan accommodations and activities. Consider using hotel points for your stopover stay — Hyatt points in Istanbul or IHG points in Singapore pair well with an Aeroplan stopover. The stopover is the bonus trip, so treat it as a mini-vacation within your larger journey.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on one-way awards. This is more than enough time for a genuine visit to your stopover city. You can stay as briefly as 24 hours (anything less is considered a connection, not a stopover) or as long as 45 days before continuing to your final destination.

No. The free stopover on a one-way award is included at no additional mileage cost. Your total point cost is determined by the origin-to-final-destination pricing, not by the number of stops along the way. A flight from New York to Bangkok with a stopover in Istanbul costs the same as New York to Bangkok direct.

Aeroplan prices round trips as two one-way tickets. Each one-way award allows one free stopover, so a round-trip booking can include up to two stopovers — one on the outbound and one on the return. This effectively turns a round trip into a four-destination itinerary.

Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian, and THAI Airways impose significant fuel surcharges on award tickets that can add $100 to $400 per segment. To minimize out-of-pocket costs, route through carriers with no or low surcharges: Turkish Airlines, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines (on most routes), and United. Check the fare breakdown before confirming your booking.

Aeroplan's free stopover on one-way awards is a genuinely unique feature that no other major North American loyalty program offers. The ability to spend a week in Istanbul, Singapore, or Tokyo as a free add-on to your business class award makes Aeroplan one of the most valuable programs in the travel rewards ecosystem. Combine this with access to 26+ Star Alliance carriers, online booking for stopover routings, and 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, and Bilt, and you have a program that delivers outsized value for the ChooseFI community. Build a transferable points balance, identify your dream two-destination trip, and let Aeroplan's stopover rule turn one award into two vacations.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

It suits owners who charge under $50,000 a year and will move the points to airline or hotel programs. Owners who’d rather redeem for cash or flights booked through American Express Travel should get the Blue Business Cash, which pays 2% in cash on the same first $50,000.

#8572. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:

Every time you log into the exclusive “reviewers only” Vine website, you’ll see different stuff available for the taking. Sometimes there is almost nothing worthwhile – you’ll search for “porcelain plates” and get endless pages of pink plastic disposable party plates instead. You look for a toaster for your kitchen but instead there will be just a toaster cover with a cat wearing a witch hat. WTF!?

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well)

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

The 50-20-0% rule for used products is something on the lines of:

50% FMV for name brand products 20% FMV for off brand/non branded name products 0% FMW for things you use for “business purposes for review, are broken or damaged, and are consumables that can’t be resold after opening

From all my research and extreme warnings from my CPA, this “50-20-0%” method is not a legally recognized tax strategy and carries massive audit risk.

The products we receive are legally considered non-employee compensation given to us in exchange for the service of writing reviews.

The IRS strictly requires taxpayers to report the Fair Market Value (FMV) of this compensation at the exact moment of receipt (though in practice, Amazon’s FMV is set at tine of ordering, not receipt).

Because you take immediate ownership of the item at its full value, opening and using it to write the review is legally considered personal use. Therefore, you cannot claim business depreciation or arbitrarily lower your 1099-NEC gross income for the “wear and tear” of opening your own compensation.

My CPA explicitly stated he will not file our taxes using fabricated internet depreciation formulas to arbitrarily lower a 1099-NEC.

Here is another discussion on the TurboTax forums where someone explains exactly why you cannot use this 50-20-0 rule and that there is no accepted way to manipulate the FMV of what you receive: https://ttlc.intuit.com/community/business-taxes/discussion/amazon-vine-1099-nec-schedule-c-deductions/00/3715093

The Vine program can easily cause a significant financial impact come tax season. Because Amazon issues a 1099-NEC, the IRS system automatically assumes this is business income subject to an additional 15.3% self-employment tax. When added to a normal ~25% income tax bracket, that creates a massive tax burden. For me, even living in Texas with no state income tax, I am still looking at roughly a 40% tax burden by default, which is brutal.

You can try to claim it as a hobby to avoid that 15.3% FICA tax, but overriding a 1099-NEC, moving it from schedule C to schedule 1, requires preparation to defend since the discrepancy because it can trigger an automated CP2000 notice.

For context, last year Amazon sent me a 1099-NEC with a massive $38,000 FMV for all my 2025 Vine items. (yes, the curse of making gold which means much more allowance and expensive >$100 items, such as a $1500 Gigabyte laptop amd $1k mini split AC, and a lot of other expensive gold exclusive items)

My CPA does not want to use the hobby declaration for that $38k because the sheer volume and daily review time makes it very hard to defend, even though I have not sold anything.

Beyond the tax classification, you must be extremely careful about Amazon’s published FMVs because they are often wildly inflated. Sometimes if you wait a few months, you will find that you could have purchased the exact same product outright for less cash than you are paying in tax liability through Vine.

This is why I am giving the warning that you have to do your homework before choosing things, sivh as checking price history and comparing to similar products. Buying outright means you only buy what you actually need, the item can be returned if you don’t like it, has a real warranty when it breaks, and you do not have to waste 30-60 mins writing a detailed review.

For example, I ordered a cold press juicer, even though I already own about nine other juicers, assuming the FMV was fair. I figured getting it for 40 cents on the dollar was a good enough deal. A few months later, the retail price dropped by about 75%. I ended up paying more in taxes for an un-warrantied, non-returnable item that I wasted an hour reviewing than if I had just bought it outright down the road.

In another instance, I selected a frozen drink slushie machine with an almost $300 FMV, meaning $120 in taxes for me. I spent a lot of time reviewing it, put it away, and then pulled it out months later to actually use it and found it was not freezing properly. I attempted to contact the seller but Amazon simply stated there is no warranty on a “free” product, making my $120 tax cost completely irrelevant. I also found that they replaced that product with a near identical model at a much lower, more competitive price.

I do not believe you can safely claim depreciation the way others have said, and even claiming hobby status to avoid the extra 15.3% FICA means going directly against Amazon’s 1099-NEC filing, requiring you to be ready to defend it. That said, I am now a much wiser Vine participant. I only select items that either have a $0 FMV or a very good one that is actually at or below actual value, and only if they are items that I actually need.

Actually, you don’t take “ownership” of the item until the 6-month mark, when you get the right of disposition, (if you cannot sell it nor give it away, you don’t own it). Before that the non-consumable item is the property of Amazon that you have been contracted to use & review in return for the compensation of the item in question at that 6-month mark. The item carries no value to you until then and when it does become yours, it’s value is depreciated from whatever FMV Amazon may set for a “new” item by virtue of its being used.
