#8551. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Adventure Has No Retirement Age: Adventure is continuing well into the ninth decade of life for a growing number of paddlers and hikers. Ninety-one-year-old Dale “Greybeard” Sanders only took up extreme endurance challenges at 80. Since then, he has paddled the Mississippi River from source to sea twice, completed the Missouri River Race, and this year reclaimed the record as the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail.

The challenge of competing and breaking records keeps him going, but not everyone is chasing endurance records. For Wendy Eden, 77, the goal is just to be out in nature and to keep exploring her beloved Canadian wilderness on her own. That means adapting her approach as she gets older.

I Hitchhiked From Sydney to Perth: Aston Brown describes his experience of hitchhiking across Australia from Sydney to Perth. He sees hitchhiking as an opportunity to surrender control and connect with people he would otherwise never meet.

Far more common in the 1970s and 1980s, the practice plummeted in Australia because of its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who targeted hitchhikers. Now it is starting to pick up again, as online communities and social media introduce it to a new generation.

Brown recognizes that hitchhiking carries dangers and that his experience as a man does not reflect the risks women traveling alone face. Yet his journey left him with a sense of connection. He spent three days and 1,900km traveling with Neil, a 79-year-old widower, on a four-month road trip around Australia. He also met a Zimbabwean family who had left the U.S. because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns, a retired tractor enthusiast, and Doug, head of Australia’s national science agency, who invited him birdwatching to see one of the country’s rarest birds.

She Had a Will To Live: A 72-year-old hiker survived six nights in the wilderness after falling 30m down a steep embankment. Mary Beth Granbery was on the Cabin Creek Trail near Mount Shasta in California when she fell.

She had set out on a multi-day camping trip and was expected home within four days. When she failed to return, friends and family raised the alarm. Rescuers found her camper van at the trailhead and launched a search. They found her one day later, at the bottom of the embankment. Despite suffering injuries from the fall, dehydration, and hypothermia from the cool nights, Granbery was still conscious when the rescue team reached her.

Across Madagascar To Find The World’s Last Lemurs: Geena Truman and her husband took a 2,500km road trip across Madagascar to search for lemurs. In a rented 4×4, they set off from Antananarivo. On the RN7 highway, they drove through rainforest, highland rice paddies, canyons, and desert, encountering rare species including golden bamboo lemurs, ring-tailed lemurs, and Verreaux’s sifakas.

Leaving the highway, they ended up on rough tracks with tricky river crossings, mud pits, and routes so difficult to navigate that they hired a local guide, known as a pisteur, to find their way.

Driving through Madagascar’s iconic baobab trees towards Tsingy de Bemaraha and Kirindy Reserve. Photo: Geena Truman

Grand Ole Roadtrip: In the summer of 1976, six young climbers piled into a blue Ford van and drove west to tackle Wyoming’s Teton Range. That first trip to the Tetons saw them face loose rock on the Enclosure Ice Couloir, a terrifying slide down the Skillet Couloir that nearly carried two of the group over a glacier’s edge, and two separate encounters with violent thunderstorms that left them clinging to exposed rock.

At the heart of all of this was the Grand Teton Climbers’ Ranch (GTRC), an affordable base for mountaineers. It offered more than a cheap bed: It was a place to meet climbing partners, exchange stories, and recover from the day over shared meals. Today, the GTRC remains one of their favorite places on Earth.

Renate Powell Completes Munro Round in Barefoot Shoes: Renate Powell has completed her second round of Scotland’s 282 Munros, this time in barefoot shoes. The keen hillwalker turned to minimalist footwear in her forties when an old skiing injury left her knee in constant pain.

She started by walking just 100m a day, then spent more than a year gradually building up to take on a Munro in her barefoot shoes. Fourteen years after first trying them, she continues her long-distance walking, without the knee replacement that was initially suggested.

Climbing the Cuillin Munro in barefoot shoes. Photo: Gillian Parker

Mad, Bad and Dangerous To Know: Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, has been living with Parkinson’s for seven years. He’s been out of the public eye for two years, and his current state is uncertain.

Fiennes spent much of his life building a remarkable expedition career after serving in the military. His 1979-82 Transglobe Expedition saw him and fellow former SAS soldiers Charles Burton and Oliver Shepard complete a 60,000km circumnavigation using surface travel, crossing both Poles.

He later completed a 2,170km unsupported ski crossing of Antarctica with Mike Stroud, and attempted to reach the North Pole unsupported five times. After severe frostbite during a 2000 expedition, he famously amputated his own dead fingertips with a fretsaw. This article plots out the timeline of his extraordinary expeditions.

A Climber Has Now Called For Help Three Times in 2026: Two climbers had to be rescued on September 22 after becoming stranded on the 500m White Dyke scramble on British Columbia’s Edge Peak. The pair set out at 8:30 am, but later that afternoon, with only three hours until sunset, the less experienced climber was too exhausted to continue.

After two hours attempting to rescue themselves, they activated a Garmin SOS beacon. This is the third time one of the climbers in the duo has had to be rescued this year. Rescue veteran Brent Boulet warned that social media seems to be drawing less experienced people onto technical routes. He stressed the importance of realistic timing, turning back when necessary, and knowing a climbing partner’s capabilities before setting out.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8550. Controversy Continues on Dhaulagiri as Expeditions Called Off

After Manaslu, Dhaulagiri is the second 8,000’er this season with no summits. The rope-fixing team says they stopped working for safety reasons, but some climbers suspect other motivations and describe a tense atmosphere.

Paul Clarke of Australia — who had been waiting at Camp 2 for five days — shared his frustrations with ExplorersWeb. Clarke had just learned that the rope fixers had stopped working above Camp 3 and were retreating. He described a lack of motivation among the Sherpa rope fixers after VIP clients with Seven Summit Treks, the company in charge of fixing the route, had called off their summit attempt. Soon after, all 20 climbers waiting at Camp 2 were told to return to Base Camp.

“Makalu Lakpa came through the lower camp this morning after the decision had been made,” Clarke said. “It was a pretty uncomfortable atmosphere, and I think everyone understands just how badly this has affected the rest of the teams on the mountain.”

Clarke’s outfitter, 8K Expeditions, sent a Sherpa team to retrieve their gear and tents from Camp 3 at 7,100m.

A helicopter lands at Dhaulagiri Base Camp. Photo: Paul Clarke/@outdoorpirate

Makalu Lakpa Sherpa is leading the 14 Peaks Dhaulagiri Expedition, one of the two largest teams, together with its sister company, Seven Summit Treks. Today, he posted a message explaining that increasing winds on October 10 resulted in a higher risk of slab avalanches on October 11, when his team was due to attempt the summit. He says that is the only reason his team returned to Base Camp.

In an unusual remark, Lakpa stated that he looks after his own group and cannot be held responsible for “other teams’ summit ambitions, climbing strategies, or rope-fixing arrangements.” He also noted that the rope-fixing work was assigned to Seven Summit Treks, not his team.

Finally, he spoke out against climbers who had expressed their disagreement yesterday:

To those criticizing our decision from a distance, I ask you to understand the actual mountain conditions before passing judgment. Assessing risks firsthand and making decisions that determine whether a team returns home safely is very different from commenting on social media.

Guides working for Lakpa’s company and for Seven Summit Treks have posted messages on social media supporting his decision. Benny Lieber, an American guide working for 14 Peaks, posted his assessment of avalanche risks on the mountain:

A post on Dhaulagiri conditions by Benny Lieber on Instagram. Photo: Benny Lieber/Instagram

Chhang Dawa Sherpa, leader of Seven Summit Treks, argued that the weather window was too short, given that a summit push would take “several days.” The plan was to move up to Camp 3 on October 11, reach the summit on the morning of October 12 (with October 13 as a buffer day), and return to Base Camp the following day.

Chhang Dawa, a director at Seven Summit Treks, posted about Dhaulagiri’s weather forecasts. Photo: Chhang Dawa/Instagram

Still, these explanations have not satisfied some climbers. Their biggest frustration came from watching the mountain in perfect, windless weather (though a wind plume eventually grew on the summit, according to Benny Lieber).

“From my perspective, one of the biggest frustrations is how badly the weather window appears to have been misread by Makalu Sherpa,” Paul Clarke said. “The strong winds and poor climbing conditions yesterday were not a surprise, since we had all been watching the forecasts for days, and winds in the 40–50kph range had been clearly visible well in advance.

“Despite that, Makalu Sherpa sent the rope-fixing team and his VIP clients higher on the mountain yesterday in conditions that were obviously going to be difficult. That has left climbers from multiple other operators stranded by a decision they had no control over. The consequence is that the rope-fixing team has now come back down, the VIP clients are no longer continuing [a helicopter was waiting for them as they arrived in Base Camp], and we have just been told that all our expeditions are over.”

Vincere Zeng of Singapore also shared her pòint of view with ExplorersWeb. Zeng has summited seven 8,000’ers, and was the first Singaporean woman to summit K2 and Annapurna. “I attempted it [Dhaulagiri] last autumn as well, so I was fully aware of the risks involved, which is why I had been monitoring the weather closely every day,” she said.

Zeng explained that her group was aware of high winds on October 9 and 10, and therefore waited at Camp 2. They planned to attempt the summit today, on October 12, in the morning. “We also considered Oct 12-13 as a possible buffer, as the next strong wind cycle was forecast to arrive around the afternoon of Oct 14,” Zeng explained.

“What I did not understand was why the 14 Peaks team chose to move toward Camp 3 (~7,000m) on Oct 10, which was the windiest day in the forecast, and then cancelled the rope fixing based on the conditions they encountered that day,” Zeng said. “From our side, we hoped we would at least have the opportunity to assess conditions during the originally planned Oct 11-12 window.”

Both Clarke and Zeng said that the 8K Sherpas who went to Camp 3 yesterday to retrieve equipment reported good conditions to that point.

“Of course, that does not mean conditions higher up, particularly around the traverse and summit slopes, were necessarily safe,” Zeng noted. “But it was one reason I hoped conditions could be reassessed once the forecasted wind had passed, especially as we still had time to do so. Instead, we were informed that the expedition was cancelled before we had that opportunity.”

Vincere Zeng (with green down suit) waits at Camp 2 in good weather last weekend. Photo: Vincere Zeng

Zeng explained she was “absolutely prepared to turn around if an assessment showed that conditions were unsafe.”

Clarke confirmed that all commercial expeditions on Dhaulagiri have called off their attempts. With the big teams pulling out, there is no manpower to launch another commercial-style attempt.

“At this point, nearly all of the teams have already packed up their Base Camp operations, and almost all of the climbers have flown out by helicopter, either yesterday afternoon or this morning,” Clarke said.

One team, however, has no intention of leaving. Andrzej Bargiel’s expedition, which includes a significant support team and film crew, is still hoping to summit and ski down the mountain, as he explained to fellow climber Xenia Santha of Hungary today.

“We wish Andrzej [Bargiel] the best of luck,” Clarke said. “If he can continue and summit, it will obviously provide another very clear picture of what the conditions on the mountain were actually like during this window.”

Risk assessment is always a tricky issue on commercial expeditions. Climbers pay large sums of money and expect every possible summit chance. It is often hard to explain when conditions are too risky, considering that factors include avalanche risks and wind, but also group sizes, the skills and endurance of guided climbers, complex logistics, and the disastrous consequences of a wrong decision.

However, in this instance, it is the lack of choices rather than the conditions that has frustrated climbers. Ironically, commercial expeditions on big mountains are more interdependent that ever, but communication between them, and sometimes with their clients, can be poor.

“As a client, I have no exact knowledge of the rope-fixing arrangement or collaboration agreed between the different outfitters,” Zeng said. “As we were a relatively small team with less manpower [8K Expeditions], we were to some extent dependent on the main rope-fixing team and whatever cooperation had been agreed between the operators. So, once the main fixing effort stopped, in practical terms it also affected our ability to continue.”

“Seven Summit Treks and Makalu Lakpa are now, from our perspective, trying to justify the decisions that were made by saying the weather was the reason they stopped,” Clarke concluded after reading the posts by Makalu Lakpa and Chhang Dawa today. “Based on the forecasts we had been watching for days, what we saw ourselves, and now the reports from climbers and Sherpas who were actually higher on the mountain, I simply don’t agree with that explanation.”

Large expedition operators sometimes react only when climbers openly share their experiences and thoughts, and their reaction is often to try to stop the dissemination of news from the mountains.

Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha, said media coverage had caused tension. Santha received a text message asking why she and Clarke had been speaking to the press. “I found that quite surprising; we have only spoken publicly about what we experienced firsthand and about decisions that directly affected our expedition,” Clarke said.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly free — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. #8548. A Human-Powered Journey Around Norway

Bad weather has forced Norwegian Jonas Holm, 27, to alter his 5,500km human-powered attempt to circle Norway.

Holm took a year off from his construction job and set out from southern Norway in late April, beginning in Svinesund on the Swedish border. He planned to paddle nearly 3,000km north, skirting Norway’s coastline as far as Grense Jakobselv, near the Russian border. From there, he would travel south through Norway, Finland, and Sweden with his dog, Rago.

Jonas Holm during the kayak section of his journey. Photo: Jonas Holm/Padling

However, difficult conditions forced him to stop paddling south of Bodø in northern Norway, a little over halfway to Grense Jakobselv. On his website, Holm says he wants to avoid feeling pressure to reach particular places by particular dates, instead focusing on experiencing the landscape. With constant wind and rain, he decided the remaining fiords could wait until next spring.

Holm’s tracked route so far. Photo: Jonas Holm

Holm won’t sit on the couch until he can complete the coastline. Rather than wait months for better weather, he has stored his kayak and will begin the second segment of his journey: the 2,500km trek south from Grense Jakobselv. After a quick break at home to dry his clothes and gear, Holm recently drove north to Grense Jakobselv and set out with a backpack and a companion. Rago, his Alaskan malamute, is even carrying some equipment. As winter arrives and snow accumulates, Holm plans to eventually transition from walking with a backpack to skis and a pulk.

His exact route is unclear, but he will roughly trace Norway’s eastern border, though he mentions crossing parts of Finland and Sweden on his way back to his starting point in southern Norway.

You can follow Holm’s progress through the live tracker on his expedition website.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8547. You Won’t Be Able To Spend Your Money When You’re Old

If you wait too long to start spending your money, you will have wasted many years of unnecessary work, stress, and worry. You'll have traded your best decades for a number on a screen that eventually gets passed to someone else.

After another summer living with my parents, I'm even more convinced about 45, my recommended start of decumulation. Not because the math changed, but because I watched the alternative up close for two summers in a row.

Here's the realization: you won't be able to spend all your money when you're old. Not “you shouldn't.” You won't be able to. The ability and the desire itself disappears.

And when I say old, I'll peg that age at 65+, the traditional retirement age when corporations no longer deem you productive enough to keep around.

If you want to get a glimpse of how you'll be when you're old, simply spend more time with your parents when they're old. After all, children are highly influenced to follow in their parent's footsteps in many stages of life. Spending time with your elderly parents will give you a clue as to how you’ll be when you’re their age.

My parents used to love going on cruises to various parts of the world. It was one of the ways they enjoyed their wealth in retirement.

Then COVID hit and their cruising enthusiasm never came back. When I asked them why they don't go anymore, they said they can't be bothered. They also don't want to risk getting sick.

So I offered to pay. A nice cruise, balcony suite, any duration, any location. My treat.

They declined. This makes me sad as I fondly reminder seeing the joy on both my parent's faces every time they went to the buffet.

The single largest barrier to spending money, the money itself, was removed entirely. And they still said no.

Upon second thought, maybe money isn’t the biggest hurdle since they have pensions. It’s simply just their lack of interest and their desire to stay healthy.

One of my favorite childhood memories was going to Hanauma Bay with my father. We walked down and up the hill no problem. We even ran into Robin Williams. But when I decided to take my own kids for the first time this trip, I already knew he wouldn't want to come, so I didn't even ask.

Instead, he enjoys hours of free TV programming at home. My mom does too.

So I feel great knowing I bought them the largest new TV that would fit on their stand. For over a year, they had been watching a blurry TV, and just chalked the image up to poor eyesight.

But even the finest 60″ TV from a retailer now costs under $1,000. So cheap for years of entertainment.

Not one to give up easily on finding fun things my father can do with us, I first got him to play Monopoly Junior with my son and daughter. That worked until my boy lost interest after the first game. Then my daughter chucked a game piece on the ground after losing a second time. Monopoly Junior is almost entirely luck, so it stops being fun pretty fast.

The second evening, I switched to chess, a game my father used to play constantly. He was enthusiastic, and so were the kids. One of my fondest memories is playing him about 10 years ago after snow bowls for dessert. This time it was my dad versus both kids. They had a lot more fun, even though they still got crushed.

Each game cost about $20 at Target. They will be played dozens of times.

That's the entertainment budget of two people in their 70s and 80s with no debt and pensions. Board games and a TV antenna, not even cable. The rest of their spending is food, taxes from required minimum distributions, house maintenance, and property taxes.

The travel and the big-ticket experiences are simply gone.

Here's the part that makes it worse. My parents have been frugal their entire lives.

They didn't become careful with money after they retired. They were careful at 30, at 40, at 50, and by the time they hit their 70s, thrift wasn't a strategy anymore. It was part of their DNA.

We spend so much time talking about how compounding works on the asset side. Nobody warns you that it also works on the behavior side. Forty years of telling yourself “no” builds a muscle that gets very hard to relax.

You can hand a lifelong saver a spreadsheet showing they can safely spend $50,000 more a year and they will still hesitate over a $12 shave ice. The number doesn't matter. The wiring does.

This is the cruel joke of the FIRE movement that nobody puts on a chart. The exact discipline that gets you to financial independence is the thing that prevents you from enjoying it.

I have friends worth eight figures who still won't upgrade their 11-year-old car with electrical gremlins. They aren't being smart. They're being trapped by a version of themselves from 1998 who genuinely couldn't afford it.

When you're younger, it's easy to say your life will look different from your parents' when you get to their age. Then you catch yourself doing the exact same things.

I remember when my dad was 49, because I was 17, finishing up my senior year of high school and getting into a fair amount of trouble. He worked a regular job and came home with my mom around 5:30 or 6pm.

So we're different in that respect. I stopped working a day job five years before we had our son.

But I forgot that my dad and I used to play golf together whenever I came home to Honolulu. That hasn't happened in about 10 years. He lost interest and physical mobility. There was no longer enough time or motivation to get out there.

Here's the thing. I don't find golf that fun anymore either after being infatuated with the sport in my 30s. I only go when someone invites me to a corporate outing or their club, which is only two or three times a year. I'd rather play pickleball and tennis, but my body is wearing down too with increasing injuries.

Since graduating from college in 1999, I've never gotten into the habit of watching more than two hours of TV a day. Most days I watch none, just short video clips online. After all, I cut cable, remember this year. A long time ago I decided producing content was more fun than consuming it. It was also more profitable.

But if I don't end up watching a lot of TV as my cheap entertainment, I'll probably just play pickleball, go to the beach, or go hiking instead. Surprise surprise, all of those are free.

So when I was facing a liquidity crunch and my wife wanted us to vacation in Las Vegas, I decided to YOLO. I wasn't going to let my silent stress keep us from a memorable experience.

My parents drive a 28-year-old car. That means my dad has been driving the same vehicle since he was 54 and I was 21. At 49, I'm not that far behind. I've had my 2015 car, bought a year old, for 10 years now.

I could easily see myself keeping my next car until it disintegrates. The thrill of owning a fancy new car died for me around age 32. Now I want reliable, safe, and roomy enough for a family of four. Once both kids are out of the house, I'm not sure I'll need to buy anything nicer. I only drive 6,300 miles a year as it is.

Finally, my parents live in a paid-off home my grandparents built in the 1980s, after tearing down the previous house that was infested with termites. The house is too big for them, but it's great when we visit, especially now that I've finished remodeling the two-bedroom in-law unit.

Unless they want to move into a two or three-bedroom condo with amenities, they aren't spending money on property either.

We found our forever home in San Francisco after climbing the property ladder for 20 years. We won't be upgrading if we stay in the city. If we move to Honolulu, we might buy a cheaper house since prices are more affordable there.

Hmm. Almost every single line is me becoming my father, just on a 33-year delay.

Ages 65 to 70 is not that old, assuming your health is intact. But I've clearly watched my parents slow down after 70. Maybe there are being extra cautious due to the high cost of eldercare. I need to ask.

Besides yummy food and fitness, there is genuinely nothing money can buy them that brings more joy. The only thing I came up with is hiring a reliable house cleaner once a month for $500. And even that would come out of their cash flow, not savings or investments.

Which means the only way my parents will ever decumulate their wealth is through a bear market. A decline that provides them nothing in return. That's it. That's the exit.

Their money will not be spent. It will simply be transferred, either to the market on a bad year or to me and my sister.

But, I don't want it. I have my own money. I built my own thing specifically so I would never have to think about theirs. Every dollar they don't spend is not a dollar I'm quietly rooting for. It's a massage they didn't get, a cruise they didn't take, a business class seat they suffered through coach to avoid.

I'd trade the entire remainder for two more good years of them enjoying themselves.

So when I look at my life at 49, and at their lives after retiring in their 60s, it becomes obvious that there's only about a 15-20-year window to spend money intentionally.

You don't want to spend heavily before 45, because there's too much life left and probably dependents to care for. But after 45, it's go time. That window closes faster than anyone expects, and it closes from the inside.

If you FIREd well before 65, ironically, you may need to spend even more aggressively. You accumulated enough capital to retire early in the first place, which means you benefited more from the bull market than the average worker who can't live off investments alone.

A 4% or even 5% safe withdrawal rate has simply been too conservative since 2012. Your net worth is far higher than when you first retired.

After observing my parents in detail for two straight summers, I'm going to work harder at consumption spending.

I tried my best with the $40,000 earmarked for the Summer YOLO Fund and failed spectacularly, spending only 20% of it. But I still spent more than I would have without setting an intentional target, so the exercise wasn't a total waste.

I also used the remaining funds to invest in Mezzi, the AI investment advisor I think is incredibly helpful.

America generally thinks spending money on private school is a waste. I don't, so that expense is covered. My home is set for now, though I'm considering something nicer in Honolulu.

What's left is upgrading my car, eating absurdly expensive food I don't need, and donating more to charity.

I've also got to stop treating investing like a luxury expense. Investing has been one of my biggest hobbies for the past 30 years, and it's almost impossible to stop. It brings me so much joy!

Finally, I'd love to live long enough to see and help take care of my grandchildren. Hence, more money to physical and mental health.

Ironically, my parents seem happy. Or maybe the better word is content.

If you asked them whether they're missing out on anything, they'd look at you like you asked whether they're missing out on scuba diving. Not at all.

Maybe I'm projecting. Maybe I'm looking at their life through the eyes of a 49-year-old with a functioning body and a to-do list, and mistaking a calmer life for a lesser one.

Or maybe contentment is just what a lifetime of frugality feels like from the inside, and there's no way to tell the difference between peace and adaptation from the outside.

For myself, the lesson is simpler. Front-load the spending after age 45. Do the trip while your knees work. Buy the thing while you still want things.

Because the money will absolutely still be there at 75. You're the part that won't be.

Have you watched a parent become unable to spend their money, even when they clearly could afford to? At what age did the shift happen?

If you're a lifelong saver, what's the largest purely discretionary purchase you've made in the past year, and how long did you agonize over it?

Do you believe you'll spend more freely in retirement than your parents did, or is that the same thing every generation tells itself at 49?

One reason lifelong savers can’t spend is fear. What happens to my family if something happens to me? So we hoard, just in case.

Term life insurance is one of the cheapest ways to take that fear off the table. Once your family is protected, every dollar you spend on a trip, a nicer meal, or a better car stops feeling like a dollar stolen from your kids’ future.

Policygenius makes it easy to compare quotes from top-rated insurers in one place, so you can find the right coverage at the best price.

Protect your family first. Then go enjoy your money while you still can.

If you want to know how much you can actually spend down without running out, you need to see everything in one place first. I've been using Empower's free financial tools since 2012 to track my net worth, x-ray my portfolio for hidden fees, and run their Retirement Planner. The planner is what convinced me my safe withdrawal rate was too conservative in the first place.

Most people spend too little in retirement because they've never modeled what “too much” would actually look like. Run the numbers and find out where your real ceiling is. It's free to sign up and takes about 10 minutes to link accounts.

If you link over $100,000 in investable assets, you can schedule a free financial review with a professional. I've done so three times in the past 14 years, and each time has been helpful in highlighting potential blindspots to help me build more wealth. I'm not currently a client, but an affiliate.

You made me laugh out loud with “the look of joy on your parents faces at the buffet”. I think you just described me. So much truth in your article. I’m frugal, my parents were frugal, my grandparents were frugal. It’s in the DNA. I barely use my pension income, let alone investment returns. So far, at the age of 71, still interested in travel. Usually do it independently, no tours or cruises. My excuse for frugality, is the desire to leave my daughter an inheritance, because the world kind of sucks. But that’s an excuse, I’m just plain cheap. Maybe, your parents could be convinced to go on a cruise or tour if every single detail is handled for them? Sometimes it’s the planning/logistics that’s exhausting.

I’m in this phase right now. I retired at 57 which is early but not as early as I would have liked. Still I feel grateful. I’m having to spend a bit more aggressively than I’m comfortable with but we did this year! This article is well aligned with my thinking and also “Die with Zero” which is one of my favorite financial books (and also my strategy/plan). I think it might be interesting for you to consider writing some articles about other related topics that overlap.

This is one of my favorite articles ever! I do have saved and saved and have more than enough… But to ask myself, what do you want? I’m recently Widowed in a weird weird spot. And mostly I don’t know what I want. But I do enjoy spending time with my kids and going on trips with them and I think I’ll do more of that. As well as mostly hobbies, but they are almost free…

You are right we’re just accumulating. I never thought of it. I have a hard time not living in scarcity. I love your post and I love when you make us think about our lives and our income. Thanks, Sam.

Hi Kelly – Thanks for commenting and glad this post resonated with you. I’m sorry for your loss. I’m glad you’re spending time with your kids and going on trips. So much precious time gets wasted on accumulating more money we don’t need.

Preaching to the choir Sam. I just dropped about $3k on LA Phil/LA Opera/Hollywood Bowl/Ballet tickets for the next year and spend about $3k/year on French lessons with zero regrets and a fullness of life.

I just had to click on this article, as I’m living it. I’ve been on my own pretty much since age 16 and I’m 66 now. After a very early career in IT, I worked as a DOD contractor for a employee owned company for 35 years. I had a serious conversation with myself about 10 years ago after my divorce. I decided what I really wanted from life, was to not have to work. I was already living well below my means and investing the rest. Every raise went to the 401k and the Roth catchup until it was maxed for the year. I lived on the same paycheck amount for 10 years. I own 3 vehicles all with over 190k miles, the newest being ia 2013 Honda Pilot. Any extras I wanted I paid for from my side business selling antiques, collectibles and junk, so I’m addicted to picking / treasure hunting. My job was extremely stressful as mistakes could cost warfighter lives. The treasure hunting became diversion therapy for the stress. But eventually my stress induced high blood pressure pushed me to retire In August of 2023. The market dropped significantly right after and I had left a highly compensated (for the East Coast) position. I was able to work from home with great benefits. But I got to where even dialing in to a daily 9AM meeting was just too much. Since retiring, I have taken 4 specialty music cruises and been on several trips around the US. I’m planning another cruise in January and an Italy trip of 2 weeks alone. Then I will meet friends in Sicily where we have rented an ocean villa for a month. Both of those trips I’ve pretty much paid for in advance. My tax preparer asked why I pulled so much money out last year. I told her I understand the ramifications of IRMA and increased tax brackets. But that’s what I saved the money for. Even with over 3 years of spending, I still have quite a bit more than when I retired. So I just bought myself another home in North Myrtle Beach. I plan to use the home as my base in between travel. I mortgaged it to the hilt as I know I won’t be even trying to pay it off. My house in Virginia is paid off and I’m trying to determine if i want to turn it into a VRBO or sell outright. I’m leaning to VRBO so that I can stay there on visits up to see friends and doctors. I’m eyeing a new Low Speed Vehicle for beach trips as I’m only a mile from the ocean. I probably need to upgrade my SUV. Then I get down to Myrtle and instead of buying all new furniture, I find myself finding bargains on Marketplace and having friends help me retrieve the items. Investing like treasure hunting is in my DNA and it can be very hard to pay full price!

I’m sort of in the same boat but on the West Coast… Enjoy the treasure hunts. Have a wonderful time on the cruise.

Sounds like a wonderful life! Same boat, different coast

Great article! It has really made me think. Both my parents did not do much in their later years – not even travel. My Mom liked to be at home, and she had a beautiful home. She did not have a lot of income, but she really enjoyed her life with friends and doing the things she loved like creating art after my parents divorced in their mid-50’s. My Mom lived to be 93, and lived in her own home until her death. My Dad is now 97. He is frugal and reluctant to spend on himself, even though it would make his life so much easier in a lot of ways.

I am now in my mid-50’s, still working. I could retire (financially), but I am hanging on for 2-5 more years for various reasons. I do like my job for the most part. However, I am now noticing that the older I get, I like to stay home rather than travel!

I like doing gardening, going for walks, reading, running, visiting friends/family and learning about personal finance/retirement/investing. All of those things are mostly free/inexpensive! So, maybe I already have saved “too much”. And, now, thanks to this article, I realize that maybe I am going to end up just like my parents!

Great article once again and you have captured the go-go, slow-go and no-go phases of retirement perfectly. The point is enjoy the heck out of the go-go phases and if you work for the man till your 65-67 you’ve already worked past them!

What I would say is that while your consumption declines as you age, your giving can increase. You can offset the decline in consumption with a systematic increase in giving. It can be to family, friends or your favorite charities. Medical research is my favorite because I get to see the impact of the money. I also donate heavily to Tunnels to Towers which builds homes for disabled veterans and first responders killed in the line of duty.

We work so hard to save and invest systematically and many people are very wired to not spend but it doesn’t have to be that way. You can put giving and spending on autopilot by using ratios. Give and spend systematically!

but the way you worded: “builds homes for disabled veterans and first responders killed in the line of duty”.

A dead person cant live in a home. Im assuming that cause/charity builds home for the surviving families of the deceased and thats what you meant to say.

I’m 55. Retiring at year end. I work in financial services and see many of my peers and colleagues who have done very well, probably better than me, sticking around for “one more year”. It makes me feel like an outlier or that I am missing something. My decision was based on the exact points you made in the article – health and time become more valuable with each year that ticks by. The math says I’m good to go, the mental aspect is more challenging than I anticipated.

omg – this quote: We spend so much time talking about how compounding works on the asset side. Nobody warns you that it also works on the behavior side. Forty years of telling yourself “no” builds a muscle that gets very hard to relax.

Wow. Great article. So many well worded, thought provoking concepts and truth here. This is one to be read over and over again. Thank you for sharing this one!

This is one of your better articles. I may feel that way because we are thinking long and hard about retirement. We are both 62 and have run our business for the last 25 years. I have put it on the market recently and have found there are a large number of buyers that do not have sufficient cash to put toward equity at the close. I have a financial background and find it hard to comprehend. I brought 45% to the closing table when I purchased the company. Once we sell, our liquid investments should exceed $8mil.

Even with that nest egg, I am not confident in having sufficient annual growth to cover my desired living expenses. College football and basketball are my drug of choice. Additionally, I am a huge tennis fan and want to attend 3 of the 4 majors annually, which is no small outlay.

After saving for 40 working years, I am finding it terribly difficult to be “ok” with large spending outflows. One would think that the next egg should produce 700k annually and I don’t spend over 400k today. Still, it is hard for me to get past the feeling like I need another 2mil in liquid investments to truly be on the safe side of the hill.

I find it amazing that I feel this way. I never (until the last 7 years) believed I would have anywhere near 10mil in investments…and yet, here I am.

You shouldn’t retire if you absolutely don’t want to. The main impetus for many people to do so at your income and wealth is due to a death of a friend or a family, or a healthcare of their own. Then the focus focuses on spending the best time when the healthiest on whatever they want.

And I’ll tell you that getting to $10 million will not change your life. And if you keep grinding to $15 million, or $25 million, your life won’t change either.

The health can fall off a cliff at any moment. So I would be more intentional with your spending if you can.

I retired in June 2025. The largest discretionary expense we made was when we bought another house in another state on a whim. A friend from college had just moved there and invited us to check it out. So we did. Bought a house and moved there within 3 months. The house was listed at $435K and we put 50% down, so about $220K. Didn’t hesitate for a single minute. We kept our original house which has been paid for since 2019 and our adult kids are caretaking the house for us. Also, we’re traveling to Korea to visit our son. He’s teaching English there for a year or two. That trip will cost about $15K. Not really an issue financially. We were aggressive savers while building companies.

Cool. What is your age to help us understand spending by age? Thx

I was 59 when I retired and my wife was 57. We had sold an IT services business after 20 years. We still have small residential rental management company. I realized that I had been working and supporting myself 100% since I was 19 (40 years of work!), so it was time to stop. When we retired, our net worth was about $5.5M… no sense in continuing the grind. Not sure if that counts as “retiring early”… lol

I spend way more than my parents ever did for all the reasons you’ve laid out. Some of this is generational mindset — my wife and kids love adventurous travel and once-in-a-lifetime experiences (e.g. exploring Singapore and staying at the Marina Bay Sands), while my parents would say “too far away and too fancy.”

I like the go-go, slow-go, no-go framework but I am very mindful that anything past age 65 is in the “You-Just-Don’t-Know Years”. I’ve seen people thrive and jet-set from 65-80, and I’ve seen people experience rapid decline. It’s a crapshoot! So for me, the goal is to plan financially for indefinite go-go years. It’s about always having the option. If life happens and we can’t go-go anymore, we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it but I’m not going to plan for no-go.

It really is a crap shoot after a certain age. My greatest shocks have been how quickly life can disappear once you get an illness.

Yuen specifically thinking about my father’s friend who was golfing one day and gone within six months after a diagnosis.

your revised chart with GO-GO until 55 fits pretty well with me. Retired at 53. Bought an adventure van at the start of COVID. We still have it and use it a lot. My wife and I have travelled globally extensively for pleasure and for work prior to retirement. We still do, although she’s still genuinely excited to do so more than I am these days. 59 now. She’s 63. In my case I still “get up and go” a lot. Mostly because I can and I fortunately have a circle of friends that are active and adventurous, so I go along to enjoy the camaraderie and activity. That said, in between those types of frequent trips, I thoroughly enjoy peace and quiet more than ever. As for spending, I still deliberate extensively even though there’s no actual financial reason to. I guess it’s habit more than anything…..and to minimize taxes! But if I do want something I do get it. Like a new (to me) Ferrari I don’t need. It’s a terrible financial decision and I consistently debate keeping it or selling it. It’s a ton of fun to drive on the one hand, but a costly one on the other. Affording it is zero issue financially. It just seems a bit much and really doesn’t get driven often since we travel so frequently. Anyway, just to say that I am allowing myself to spend a bit after working, saving, and investing since I was a kid, and having some fun while I can. :-). I definitely see myself slowing down over the next decade or so, just as your chart implies. In the mean time I’m trying my best to keep “doing things while I can” and enjoying family and friends as much and possible while I’m still young(ish)!

Great job going on an adventure after age 55! The time went quick, hasn’t it?

Can you give an idea of your net worth? Thx

Yes, time flies. Faster and faster the older we get it seems. A good reminder to “do it now, while we can”. This summer we spent 3.5 weeks camping our way across the country in our 4×4 van from one gorgeous hiking location to another. We’re heading back out in November for another 3 weeks to camp and hike in TN, TX, and NM. It’s good simple fun. As for nw we’re in the 10-15m range. Zero debt. Our targeted annual spending budget is $10k gross each ($20k total) in effort to stay in the 24% tax bracket. A year ago we bought our “forever home” with cash. It’s turn key which allows us to lock the door and leave. Love your posts and your books! Thanks for doing what you do! :-)

Certainly spending money is not in my DNA. I am 75 wife is 72. Both retired 3 yrs ago. We are spending money but not enough to the point that I am still able to invest about $60-70K a month. That money comes from reinvested dividends and stock trading that both of us are good at. The only big ticket item we purchased in the last couple of years was a larger house we bought for cash last year and moved in recently. Putting new roof on it was another $100K. Property taxes on our properties amount to $42K/year and maintenance adds another 15K. So we live a very high high fixed cost life but beyond that we are tight on money. New couches and patio furniture will have to wait until next year. So does another cruise. Car upgrades are budgeted for 2028 and beyond. Until our old home sells hopefully this year we sit tight and count our blessings.

Wow! Being able to spend $60-$70K a MONTH at your age is enormous!

If you have kids, are they all set up with houses, retirement, etc? How about grandkids?

Is there anything you would have done differently if you rewound time 20-30 years ago?

I am always trying to look ahead to see where the blind spots are. And I really don’t want to have the capacity to reinvest that much so I’m thinking once I turn 50 next year, to just really dial it down and take it easy. The traditional retiree lifestyle. But then I realized I have a new book coming on next fall that I need to market.

Other than very high fixed cost of our residences we spend very little on ourselves. Our daughter is planning FIRE in a couple of years so most of the money will be left to our grandchildren. Anything we would have done differently 20-30 yrs ago? I don’t think so. We have always pushed everything to the max and made good financial decisions. I don’t think we could have done better given the fact that until 5 yrs before retirement our combined gross income did not exceed $200K.

Good stuff. Can you share your estimated net worth? It is helpful for context. What did y’all do for a living?

College professor with $85K highest salary. Net worth around $15M.

Awesome! Were there any particular Investments that did well for you?

How come more people earning $85,000 a year are not worth $15,000,000, 50 years later?

It seems so obvious if you just run the numbers that eventually your wealth come down to significant levels after a long enough time. But people aren’t saving and investing as much as they should.

I think it depends on the individuals. After cancer two years ago my husband and I decided to travel aggressively until we couldn’t anymore. At 69 & 88 we are currently spending 10 weeks in Barcelona, Rome & Paris. Walking an average of 5.7 miles each day and navigating 58 worn marble steps to our 4th floor flat multiple times each day. We joke with our kids that we are spending their inheritance and they are all for it.

Oh, and we just finished our “age in place” new house with everything in it that our little hearts desired.

Walking over 5 miles a day at your age is wonderful here. Very inspiring!

Was it the cancer that jolted you two to start spending, traveling, and living it up more? If so, do you think that if he did not get cancer, your life would’ve been much more frugal and less adventurous as a result?

What do you think you should’ve done differently in your 40s and 50s? Thanks for all the wisdom.

My out-of-the blue cancer at 67 just reminded us that tomorrow isn’t promised and we threw out the travel budget and go whenever we feel like it. We booked a cruise to Alaska that left in 2 weeks when our son & family said they could go that week. We keep inviting family to join us as that is our greatest joy and we know the grandkids will soon have their own interests.

I was fortunate to retire at 42 after selling a business and because of our 19 year age difference we have always been aware that we may not have the time other couples have. Happy to be celebrating 45 years this year and my 88 year old husband, with his good Norwegian genes, can out-walk me. We are less careful with money now than in the past because our portfolio has done well and we have always spent less than our income. It might make sense for us to start giving more to our heirs now beyond the 529’s etc.

Thanks for your writing. I have referred your newsletter and given your books to many and hope they get as much from them as I do.

Wonderful! And thank goodness you are cancer-free! May you and your husband have the best of health and adventures.

Thank you for reading and sharing my newsletter and work over the years.

Good piece and a strong argument for Bill Perkins’s Die with Zero framework.

In the past, you’ve mentioned that he’s a multi-millionaire nat gas trader and HF principal so his financial philosophy doesn’t broadly apply. Here, you’re more aligned.

Would like to hear your current views and if they’ve changed and/or softened.

Keep up the good work and hope you treat yourself for the big 5-0

I’ve actually been writing about decumulation well before that book came out, and he has commented and reached out to me before. After all, I started writing about FIRE in 2009 and left in 2012.

It’s a good message, but I just want people to be careful that Bill had over $100 million in net worth when that book came out and it has surely since grown. It is a luxury belief to tell people to die with zero when you have so much money.

My parents are 70 and 81 and spending more money than ever. They and their RV friends rent expensive rental pads in resorts in Florida a few months of the year ($$$) where they all play pickleball 5 days a week. They now happily outsource lawn care, cleaning, and some cooking. On top of the 100k RV that rapidly depreciates and costs a fortune to maintain.

They love spending money on cars! It helps that their money comes from pensions and social security. They would be a lot more cautious if it came from a pot of money.

At 64 (when my father was 79) my parents moved country (partly to be near my brother and their grandchildren). But after my father died at 86 years old my mother really didn’t spend much though she had almost $3 million. The biggest thing she did was buy some stamps, which were being auctioned for charity. Now I am 61 and retired but I have children aged 7 and 10. So, I’m definitely going to be spending lots of money for the next 10 years!

I think you shouldn’t just be in saving mode up to 45. Live life more consistently across the years. I was going into debt up to age 30…

Can you share your thought process of having children at ages 51 and 54? How old is your wife? Thx

Read “Die With Zero.” I too worked too long (retired at 60) and saved too much. I now plan to donate $111,000 tax free to charities every year from my IRA and it will still probably last 30 years! I recently ditched my 40-year-old Acura Integra. There’s still several million in other accounts which at even a modest 6% average growth rate will be challenging to spend down.
